subsubtopic: EXCLUSION OF PROFESSIONAL EMPLOYEES FROM BENEFITS OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
speechtext:
1.	For what reasons were professional employees on the Federal Public Service excluded from the benefits of collective bargaining under Part V of the Canada Labour Code?
2.	Is the government giving consideration to amending the Public Service Staff Relations Act to provide professional employees with a meaningful method of settling unresolved disputes?
3.	Will the government amend Section 36(1) of PSSRA to eliminate the requirement of the binding notice by the bargaining agent for arbitration or conciliation-strike as the method of bargaining to minimize the advantage it gives Treasury Board and, if not, for what reason?
4.	Will the government give consideration to (a) giving the reasons in arbitration awards (b) appointing an employee representative to the arbitration tribunal to have an input into the procedures for arbitration equal to that of the employer and, if not, for what reason?
5.	For what reasons (a) are conciliation board decisions not made binding as for arbitration tribunals (b) is there no legal provision requiring further negotiations?
6.	For what reasons are public servants denied the same rights as other citizens covered by the Canada Labour Code?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: EXCLUSION OF PROFESSIONAL EMPLOYEES FROM BENEFITS OF COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
speechtext:
1.
The Canada Labour Code, Part V does not apply to the Public Service of Canada. Collective bargaining in the federal Public Service is governed by the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Under the P.S.S.R.A. professional employees are not excluded from the benefits of collective bargaining. There are 27 certified bargaining groups in the scientific and professional category of the Public Service of Canada.
2. Yes the government has indicated its intention to improve the method of settling unresolved disputes.
3310

April 16, 1973
Order Paper Questions
3.	Under the P.S.S.R.A. as it now reads, Bargaining Agents unilaterally select the dispute resolution process that will apply to the bargaining unit for each round of negotiations. This is a distinct advantage to the union. The Treasury Board, as Employer, is bound by the Bargaining Agent's selection.
4.	(a) Under the P.S.S.R.A. as it now reads, an arbitral award becomes an integral part of a collective agreement. Reasons for the award would be superfluous to such a document; (b) A person representing the interests of the employee sits on every Arbitration Tribunal.
5.	(a) In the conciliation process there are no decisions rendered by the Board. Its purpose is to achieve agreement. If there is no agreement it so reports. The Public Service Staff Relations Act provides that after seven days have elapsed from the receipt by the Chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board of the report of the Conciliation Board, employees who are included in the dispute may participate in a lawful strike; (b) For the P.S.S.R.A. to provide for further mandatory negotiations after a Conciliation Board Report would suspend the right to strike. In fact, negotiations always do take place after a Conciliation Board Report has been received.
6.	In essence the provisions of the statutes which govern employees of the Public Service are generally no less favourable than those contained in the Canada Labour Code.

[Editor's Note: The answer to the above question follows:]
Representations have been made to the Department of National Health and Welfare regarding the levels of fluorides in mineral waters. New standards for mineral water were established by order in council P.C. 1972-3074, December 21, 1972 and published in the Canada Gazette of January 10, 1973. However, because of manufacturers' and importers' operational problems, these new standards will not become effective until September 1, 1973. A news release of December 13, 1972 stated that analyses of a limited number of mineral waters carried out by the health, protection branch of the department showed that these products contained from less than one part to more than nine parts per million of fluoride. It was emphasized then that there was no evidence to suggest that the fluo-

ride levels of mineral waters represented an immediate hazard to the health of Canadians. Officials of the department are examining all mineral waters sold in Canada for fluorides, as well as initiating a survey to determine the quantities of this beverage consumed by individuals. When these data become available, action appropriate to the findings will be taken to protect Canadian consumers of this product.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since it is now two and a half years ago that the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women was presented and evidently less than 2 per cent of the positions rated at $26,000 a year or more are held by women, may I ask the Prime Minister whether he intends to take any significant measures to remedy this situation, over and above the assurance of the President of the Treasury Board that rules and regulations will be reviewed to ensure that there is no discrimination against the female sex?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret I will not be able to answer this question in detail, but there was a statement and answers given by the Minister of Labour to questions on this subject. I am sure that he will be able to give further details if the Leader of the Opposition wants to ask him.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether the government has established any precise targets for or a definition of equitable participation of women in senior government posts?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will gladly take note of the question on behalf of the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Labour.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have asked these questions because I thought they would be of general concern to the Prime Minister and the government. I should like to ask whether the government has dismissed out of hand the establishment of precise targets in this area of senior positions for women in the Public Service? In view of the rejection by the President of the Treasury Board of any quota system, has the government rejected the establishment of precise targets to be achieved?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we dislike the quota approach to any of these problems. We would hope we would not have to use it in the case of women. This being said, every effort is being made by the government to ensure that women are considered for the appointments we make.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ACHIEVE GREATER EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN IN HIGHER POSITIONS

I would think it is particularly incumbent on the government, in a minority situation, to do some listening when transportation is being discussed. CNR and Air Canada
sive and which create employment for people in those areas.
Mr. Speaker, I have discussed at some length the whole question of the debt owed by the Canadian National Railways since they are carrying a debt which they ought not to be carrying as can be seen from this particular financing bill. A few years ago there was a change in the relationship of the debt between the Canadian National and Air Canada. There should be a further extension of that change to remove that debt from the books of the CN. After all, surely Mackenzie and those people who were shareholders back in the 1900's when the Tory party bought out those railways have been paid enough.

speechtext:
Too much. I raised the question of the freight rate structure as it relates to many regions of this country and the relationship between it and grain. I brought up very briefly the question of rail line abandonment which faces western Canada more than any other area. I suggested that in lieu of 1975 being the cut-off date in terms of allowing railroads to abandon wholesale, if you like, the rail lines in western Canada, the government ought to consider putting a moratorium on that date in order to come up with a concrete proposal to western producers. In addition, the many hundreds of thousands of people who live in these small communities deserve a concrete answer as to the kind of national transport policy they are going to have and the kind of service they are going to get from the transportation system. The government ought to take the step of letting the producer know what kind of system he is going to have for the movement of his grain, what kind of cost he is going to incur if 610 miles of line in the Assiniboia constituency are abandoned, and over 2,000 miles of line, I believe, in the province of Saskatchewan. Hundreds of smaller or middlesized communities on the Prairies are threatened by that kind of abandonment at this stage of development. I would hope that some minister of the Crown, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), or the minister in charge of the Wheat Board who likes to stick his finger into transportation, would give us some answers to this all-important question.
One other question that needs an answer concerns the closing of the station agencies. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) raised this problem in the question period, and I hope he doesn't mind my mentioning it. It affects southern Saskatchewan as well. What kind of operation is being conducted when a railroad establishes a "servo centre" working out of the two major centres in the province of Saskatchewan, Regina and Saskatoon, then says it is for additional service to the producer and the people in the smaller communities. All the station agents are removed from those areas and then the company takes the opportunity to try to explain to these communities what this service centre is? They all know what it is. It is a telephone line which can be attended to in the city of Regina at a given time by some guy in an office who answers inquiries about some service some producer needs. If the producer is lucky he might get results by the end of the month. That is the kind of servo centre which is being developed in the prairie region. That is the kind of nonsense we put up with from public and privately-owned

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
railroads in this country, and the kind of system we have when there is no national transportation policy whatsoever.
In view of the spending on transportation studies by the Canada Grains Council and such things as the notorious group called the Great Plains project, there ought to be an explanation in this House by the Minister in charge of the Wheat Board to the Members of Parliament as to the allocation of funds for those two projects and an explanation of the kind of work they are doing. The Great Plains group talks about western development. The group is made up of highly established officials of the boardrooms of large multinational corporations and national corporations. There is not one representative of the western producers included, and the group works out of the Prime Minister's office. Where is there an explanation of that particular item in this debate related to transportation?
What is going on in the Canada Grains Council when two major farm organizations, the National Farmers Union and the Wheat Pool withdraw their membership? Why did they withdraw? What is the Canada Grains Council a front for if it is not a front for the private grain exchange in Winnipeg, the friends of the Conservative party, the friends of the Tory party? I am talking about the private Winnipeg grain exchange, something we New Democrats would like to see eliminated from the grain handling business. Bring flax, rye and rapeseed under the Wheat Board and quit fooling around.
That kind of question should be answered by one minister of the Crown. There is a long list of them. For example, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, since he wants his finger in the transport pie, should explain to members of the House of Commons the agreement to pay for the expenses and the depreciation of the hopper cars which are leased to the railway. There is not a producer in the west who does not know that the railroad could improve its rolling stock. There isn't a producer in the west who does not know that the railways could use many more than 2,000 hopper cars. But there isn't a producer in western Canada who doesn't know that for a hundred years or so the old line parties have backed the railways versus the producers by way of grants and money and rates, you name it, Mr. Speaker. They know that $48 million spent on hopper cars is a kind of subsidy to the railroads. Under the Railway Act the railways have to provide proper rolling stock for the Prairies. Anyway, they are supposed to do so. Yet we have had to live with boxcars which are beyond description. So we need hopper cars, but we don't need to encourage the railways to abdicate their responsibilities to the western producer and use Canadian taxpayers' money to provide a subsidy to the railway. The minister can tell us about the agreement on that particular issue. Who is paying for it? Is the producer not paying for maintenance and depreciation of hopper cars?
We could go down a long list of questions on which I wish to spend a few moments, questions on which I am sure my colleagues will expand and to which the government should give answers during this debate on second reading of the bill before us. One of the most fundamental ones, and one which was raised again today in the House, is the question which has been asked in the past by the leader of our party relating to the future of Air Canada
[Mr. Knight.l
and landing rights in Milan. Further to this, the minister could talk about the carving up of the world in terms of the private CP line and the Air Canada line. As far as I am concerned, when it comes to air transportation and air service, Canada needs, like most of the western world countries, only one publicly-owned airline. It does not need the CP whatsoever.
Aside from that, there ought to be an explanation during this debate as to the future of Air Canada if we are to continue to put money into it. Mr. Speaker, I have raised before the question of one of the ministers of the Crown, namely, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), answering a question in relation to the CN continuing to carry a debt it should not necessarily have to carry. Further to this I suspect my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), will raise a question related to-if anyone can guess-pensions of railway workers who retired prior to 1956 and are not covered by collective agreements. That is the key point I wanted to make-those who are not covered by the collective agreements with the railroad. I am sure my hon. friend from Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) will bring up the question of freight rates, regional development and rail line abandonment and will seek some answers. I am sure my colleague from Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) will wonder about the kind of agreement that the Canadian Wheat Board and the railroads have chosen to adopt in regard to hopper cars. I am sure he will be interested in receiving answers to the questions he has asked in the House.
The hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney) will be interested in having some answers about the investment procedures used by the pension funds of the CNR and CPR, the manner in which workers' funds are used and the kind of corporations in which they are invested. In addition, I am sure the hon. member for Scarborough West will be asking questions about the CN needle, the 1,800-foot monstrosity to be erected in the city of Toronto to scare the life out of those unfortunate people from the prairies who happen to land in Toronto on their way to Ottawa.
There is one fundamental matter that concerns the Minister of Transport and I am sure my hon. friend from Saskatoon-Biggar will be interested in this question. I refer to a reinterpretation, a reassessment if you like, of the MacPherson commission report on transportation and its ludicrous proposal that what is needed is competition. What is really needed is one large public utility bent on servicing the people of Canada and not on private profit.
The hon. member for Assiniboia, as he has already pointed out, will be interested in having some substantial information about, and answers to, the question of rail line abandonment. I am sure that some of our colleagues from the maritimes and the prairie regions will be interested in having answers to questions they have asked about the future of passenger services. I am also sure the premier of British Columbia, Mr. Barrett, will be interested in some answers to questions concerning the possibility of using the railways to transport oil and gas from the Mackenzie region. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) could use this opportunity to
April 16, 1973

take a few moments to disclose to the House what possibilities there are for transporting oil and gas.
I believe the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) would like to raise in this debate some very important questions relating to the situation in the yards of the city of Vancouver, a matter I have also raised, and the question of working to rule. A number of workers there are upset about working conditions and the kind of work crews there are. Perhaps the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the Minister of Transport will take an opportunity to answer these questions.
I am sure the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and myself, both of us being members in good standing of the Hudson Bay Route Association, will be most interested in hearing what is going to happen to the port of Churchill in regard to movement of grain. Prairie members of the New Democratic Party are vitally concerned with transportation questions and are extremely interested in the possibility of the government becoming involved in the development of an alternative route through the Rocky Mountains. My colleagues have pointed out to me that my good friend and faithful colleague from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has raised questions relating to freight rates and costs in northern Ontario.
Further, I have outlined to the government a number of subject matters that call for serious consideration. If this country is to develop in a cohesive way, and if there is to be national unity, then some fundamental questions that arise in the regions of Canada must be answered. For 100 years representatives from the constituency of Assiniboia and from southern Saskatchewan have come to this House and put the case regarding the very inadequate transportation system in their area. They have described the lack of service offered by the CNR and CPR. They have discussed in this House rail line abandonment, the question of freight rate structures, the question of alternative routes through the Rocky Mountains, more adequate use of the port at Churchill, and public transportation facilities offered by Air Canada and the CNR.
It is time that the government of this country took the opportunity that is afforded to it in this minority situation, not of setting aside answers for a future debate on a CN financing bill for another year, but of outlining to Members of Parliament and the people of Canada a clear and concise national transportation policy, letting the people of western Canada and those in the regionally disadvantaged areas know what policy the government has for meeting the serious needs of national transportation.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see Bill C-164 before the House, because I have a few comments to make before it is referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. The bill is entitled, and I quote:
An Act to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways System and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973, to the 30th day of June 1974, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada.
CNR and Air Canada
Mr. Speaker, every time a bill like this is introduced, I have the impression of watching a poor comedy. For in the past, whenever we have tried to draw the minister's attention to the administrative deficiencies of the CN, and point out to him the monstrous mistakes made by the officials who administrate railways which have caused millions of dollars of damage in all kinds of derailments throughout the country, especially the province of Quebec which has the shortest railway mileage in proportion to its population and where the service leaves more to be desired than anywhere else in Canada, we have always received the impression that those in charge of the corporation wanted to cut off all passenger services in the province of Quebec, so as to get all it could in taxes from its population of over six million, and improve services in other provinces, if only by doubling its office staff, who would only be there to wait for the trains. At the rate we are going, there will be no more passenger trains in a few years because we will have managed to put off even those who are still stubborn enough to use this service.
What has been, what is and what will be the minister's response to repeated appeals and denunciations, and to the demands of the population in these areas? "The CN is a Crown corporation and I can do nothing but receive its annual report" is the minister's systematic reply. But we have reached the point where even the high-ranking officials of this company no longer need to come before the Standing Committee of Transport and Communications and condescend to keep the House informed as to what is going on in the field of transportation.
What happened during the years 1970, 1971 and 1972? And where are the 1973 estimates? I remember the time when Mr. Donald Gordon, the former president of the Canadian National, was so often called to account, and spent hours answering hon. members' questions but, at least, we had someone to give us information. Today, the president does not even dare come and face ordinary members of Parliament.
The Parliamentary Secretary of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Comtois) seems to introduce an unimportant bill whose passage according to his own words, is nothing but routine work that we should approve without any problem. That is typical of the hypocritical way the government proceeds. Besides, it is not the first time that I claim this proceeding to be improper. Every time the government introduces a bill which provides just one more dollar for the taxpayer, in services that are being claimed for years, they seem to believe that they are doing wonderful things.
I might give the ridiculous example of the $13 a month increase in the old age security pension, and the $100 yearly increase in basic exemptions for income tax purposes. You would have thought that the government was about to grant $2,000 to all Canadians. It was said that this bill was not like any other, that it would bring to the former law unsuspected amendments, that those increases were simply fantastic and a lot of publicity was made about those minor increases.
However, the same government is introducing Bill C-164 involving almost one billion and a half dollars which

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
Canadians will have to pay with their taxes. In fact, this bill will allow the CN to invest $225 million in 1973 alone and $75 million during the first six months of 1974 so as to pay, before July 1, 1974, a debt amounting to $169,500,000.
Moreover, with workers' taxes Air Canada will be paid $140 million to meet its commitments from July 1, 1973 to June 30, 1974 and a very small amount of $13 million as a guaranty on its debentures for all the rest, namely anything not involving administration since 1971 about which we have been given no detail. All this is only peanuts. In fact we are told: The House is burning down but otherwise everything is going fine. This is a picture of our puppet representatives in front of technocrats who do not give a damn about parliament as they are protected by the government.
If you read the speech of the Parliamentary Secretary of the Minister of Finance, you will find all the candor which senior civil servants can use to render the situation even more tragic.
The parliamentary secretary of the minister said and I quote:
Hon. members will remember that the 1971 bill (which included certain provisions for 1971 and 1972) had not been read for the second time when the 28th Parliament was dissolved.
This means that this bill covers 1971, 1972, 1973 and 1974, so I wonder how the Canadian National and Air Canada got the necessary funds during the past few years. And when we ask why this government has not taken any measures, why Bill C-4 has been nipped in the bud, it simply cannot lay the blame on obstruction by the opposition since it had an absolute majority in 1971.
This government was more concerned at that time by all the omnibus bills they had passed by all their "yes men" rather than introducing and having passed by this House bills which are necessary for the good operation of our country's administration.
Will the minister tell us, when this bill is considered in committee, what the government had to hide in all this matter of the CN.
It is indeed unexplainable that a Crown corporation receives such protection from government. Why was the minister not satisfied only with tabling the CN budget in previous years, without ever giving Parliament the opportunity to approve or reject it. Why did the government deliberately leave the CN money bills on the order paper after having refused to table the annual report and the auditor's report at the stage of the second reading?
As sixth objective, the parliamentary secretary of the minister announced the appointment of auditors for the years 1972, 1973 and 1974.
Mr. Speaker, I have been in business for over 30 years and it is the first time I have seen auditors appointed after three years of hiring. I have already said that if all private enterprises or the other Crown corporations used the same criteria as the Canadian National to administer themselves, they would all go bankrupt within six months. A Crown corporation can only survive because its administrative deficits are always made up by the workers' taxes and this is the principle which I have been struggling against since I first sat in the House. I do not want the
[Mr. Gauthier (Roberval).l
poor, the family head, to pay for a small group of inefficient bosses.
If Crown corporations cannot hire efficient people who decide to get to work instead of sleeping in the offices the workers have offered them with their taxes, I say these corporations should be transferred to individuals who would be able to operate them efficiently. I have already said it and I say it again, the administration of a government business costs three times that of a private enterprise. Why? Because in private business there are responsible persons who are personally interested, while nobody is responsible in a nationalized company because no one is specially concerned.
This is why the management of Crown corporations is so expensive. In addition, the technocrats who are directing the country are always too much interested in their own comfort and security to have enough time to consider the services which they should provide to the people.
In connection with those services, I hope that the minister will deem it advisable to ask the officials of the CN, including its president, to appear before the standing committee of the House, to give an account of their management and say why it is impossible to meet the responsible persons when an emergency occurs.
Last week, for example, I again witnessed an unfortunate incident. The train had left Montreal at 8 o'clock p.m. for Chambord, when it had to stop because a freight train had derailed eight miles farther. This happened at five a.m. and I was waiting, with all the others, for somebody to come to our rescue; around eight o'clock, I asked the conductor whether the authorities of the Canadian National had issued the required orders so that all passengers could reach their destination. That is when I learned that no one dared take any decision, in spite of the recommendations of the conductor and his assistants that first they had to feed the 84 passengers and then hire buses to take them back to civilization.
There were, I said, 84 passengers on the train and there was no cafeteria car between Montreal and Chicoutimi; they had removed the cafetaria car, in short, they had taken away everything. There was only a little bar where they served nothing but beer and other alcoholic beverages. That does not feed anybody, Mr. Speaker. I am telling this to hon. members so they may be aware of the stupidity of those responsible for the passenger service of the Canadian National in the Saguenay-Lake St. John area and know that this little bar is in the same car as the few bunks available on that train. Train technocrats call that a "sleeping car", Mr. Speaker, but bottles, screams, songs and music disturb everyone. I guarantee one thing, Mr. Speaker: if ever you travel on that train, you will get no sleep.
My time is almost up. Back to the derailment. I want to say that the Quebec authorities had decided, in their wisdom, not to give anything to eat to the 84 passengers and not to give bus service. Everyone was therefore condemned to spending 15 to 16 hours, in some cases even 24, waiting in the forest.
When the news came out, I took it upon myself to get in touch with the Quebec office and tell the people in charge
April 16, 1973

what I thought, adding that if the required services could not be given, I would call up Ottawa to get some action. That is when the person in charge in Quebec decided a sandwich and coffee would be made for each passenger and two buses would be sent. And so we got to Cham-bord-because we were about 100 miles from there- around three o'clock that afternoon, and in a school bus.
In passing, I would like to congratulate the train personnel for having done their best to help the passengers. But they had nothing, so what could they do?
Mr. Speaker, for many years now we have been telling the government that our area is shockingly being discriminated against as concerns transportation. In all the province of Quebec, ours is the area which brings to the Canadian National almost the largest freight revenue and yet we are unable to obtain a single sleeping car on the Montreal-Quebec line. Still, they will come to the committee and say: The service is perfect. It is so perfect that everybody is fed up and nobody wants to travel on that train. And yet, 20 years ago, we had not enough of 20 cars on that line. Today, there is one to be divided between Chambord and Dolbeau. I am saying that at the present rate, within two or three years, there will no longer be passengers because nobody will care to take the train.
I avail myself of this excellent opportunity to make all the members of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications aware of such situations.
I have provided just one example; all the derailments that have happened over the last ten years in the Sague-nay-Lac Saint-Jean area have cost millions of dollars, Mr. Speaker, not to the Canadian National but to the taxpayers of this country.
That is why I was saying a moment ago that the Canadian National authorities are practical jokers who enjoy making fun of the Canadian people. As far as I am concerned, the joke has ended. Either some cleaning has to be done in the CN or everything has simply to be sold. Let the government sell that Crown corporation to some private enterprise, and then we shall be sure to have at least equitable service adapted to the needs of the people.
Once more, I invite all the members of the committee to request its chairman to send for the responsible people as witnesses, to have them questioned and have this matter clarified once for all. Let them at least tell the committee that they have sworn to have this line disappear. Then, we shall know what to expect, and grants might be curtailed. Once more I appeal to all committee members for a serious discussions of this question.
I would have something to say about Air Canada but as there was too much to criticize about the CN, I think I will leave to others the task of dealing with Air Canada. But I want the case to be brought before the committee, to have these incompetent people appear before it in order to learn about certain things, make a clean-up and attempt to appoint at least a few qualified people.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in this debate since it affords me the chance to discuss, in a fairly general way, rail transportation problems as they affect the economic life of western Canada and, in particular, the economic life of the
CNR and Air Canada
province of Saskatchewan. Much has been written and spoken in the past by prairie groups and western Canadian politicians on the prejudicial impact the existing freight rate structure has on the resource and industry development potential of the prairie provinces. Without the availability, however, of an efficiently run rail transportation and product handling system designed to meet shipper needs, making maximum use of the advantages rail technology has on the economic development and marketing of prairie natural resources in terms of costs to the producer, any success in achieving a downward revision of the existing freight rate structure will have limited impact on prairie resource development. The level of rail freight rates, relative to other producing and consumer areas in Canada, has long been a matter of vital concern to the prairie provinces and more particularly Saskatchewan.
Saskatchewan, historically and currently, is plagued by the handicap of paying a disproportionate share of transportation costs in marketing products in common world and domestic outlets. Saskatchewan residents also pay a high price on transportation of consumer goods purchased, predominantly in the major producing areas in eastern Canada. Geographically, Saskatchewan's continental location-approximately 1,200 miles to tide water at the west and about 800 miles to the lakehead-results in the provinces' wheat producers paying the highest average rail rates on export grain, and potash producers paying the highest inland transportation cost to place potash at tidewater, compared with other world wheat and potash producers and exporters.
It is, therefore, obvious when looking at a map of Canada that Saskatchewan has a real transportation cost differential to overcome because of distance when buying and selling in major domestic and foreign markets. Distance, however, is not the only factor affecting the level of freight rates in Saskatchewan. Competitive factors are also important. The railways' practice of charging different rates for the same service has been justified by some because of competitive forces. The existence or non-existence of competition is probably the most widely applied reason for the differential price of transportation, and I accept that the railways should not be denied the right to meet competition.
There is, however, no doubt that the lack of competitive forces in parts of Canada, particularly in western Canada, has had an impact on railway revenues. The availability of water competition in eastern Canada has, from the beginning of the railway era, exerted considerable influence on the freight rate structure in that area of Canada. Saskatchewan recognizes that, to some extent, for a portion of the long hauls inbound and outbound from eastern Canada, the existence of the waterways has eased somewhat the burden of over-all costs for the movement of Saskatchewan products and consumer goods. As water competition, however, is concentrated exclusively east of the lakehead, except for the existence of transcontinental rates which benefit British Columbia and disadvantage the Prairies, the complete lack of water navigation on the Prairies places eastern Canada in a much more favourable competitive position. As compared with the situation on the Prairies, a very large proportion of the total pro-

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
ductive output in eastern Canada is moved under the influence of water competition. Practically all of the large industrial centres in eastern Canada are located on natural waterways.
Proportionally as well, the development of road transport in the east and its consequent competitive impact on the railways has benefited eastern shippers to a much greater extent than has been the case on the Prairies. The railways have been forced to establish relatively low rates in eastern Canada to meet this competition, thus placing a heavier transportation burden on prairie shippers who lack the advantages gained from the availability of this competition. The lack and dispersion of population in the prairies and the nature of the outbound traffic-relatively low value, long haul and heavy loading-is not conducive to the development of comparable trucking competition.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the west pays dearly for its position as captive shipper to the railroads. In eastern Canada, water and truck transportation pose serious competition to the railroads, and rail rates are consequently held down. But the railroads have compensated for these relatively low revenues by charging high rates in the west. Between 1948 and 1958, the rate disadvantage to prairie shippers was fostered by a series of horizontal or percentage increases authorized by the transport commissioners. The increases applied predominantly to commodities and areas lacking in alternative modes of carriage. Consequently, the prairie provinces suffer a competitive disadvantage for marketing raw and manufactured commodities in terms not only of distance to markets but of higher rates per ton mile than eastern shippers pay.
The net results has been the favouring of industry in Ontario and Quebec and the retardation, particularly of secondary industry, in Saskatchewan. The railroads have co-operated with eastern industrial interests in maintaining this disparity. The rapeseed crushing industry is a case in point. The present rate structure dictates that it costs only 65.7 cents to transport one hundred pounds of unprocessed rapeseed from Saskatoon to Montreal, while the combined cost of transporting the crushed products, oil and meal, from that one hundred pounds is 102.3 cents.
Although for a number of reasons it is more economical to produce oil and meal on the Prairies, this 34.8 cents cost differential per one hundred pounds makes it cheaper to ship rapeseed east for processing. Eastern crushers, in short, enjoy a competitive advantage due solely to the existence of discriminatory freight rates. When the prairie crushers applied to the Canadian Transport Commission for rate modifications, their application was opposed by the two railways, the eastern oilseed processors, and the province of Ontario.
Present developments in the rapeseed industry dangerously parallel the situation of the flour milling industry in eastern Canada, similarly caused by discriminatory rate structures. As a Saskatchewan Member of Parliament, I accept the point of view that our geographical disadvantage, in terms of distance to markets, is a fact to be lived with. But the west cannot be expected to subsidize low water and truck competitive rail rates in other regions of Canada where high rates prevail at the expense of diversification and development of local industry. The situation is particularly intolerable in view of the fact that the west

is largely cut off from natural trading areas to the south and across the Pacific by protective tariffs. Our agricultural produce is sold in an international competitive market, yet, we must buy the manufactured products of eastern Canada. It is patently unjust that the west be hampered with discriminatory freight rates in developing its own secondary industry.
The national policy is explicitly opposed to the exploitation of one region by another. The evident tendency of the railways to persist in instituting rates prejudicial to industrial development in the west calls for stricter government control in rate setting. From this standpoint, the national transportation legislation of 1967 which allows the railways more freedom in instituting rate changes is a step backwards. As instruments of national policy, the railways cannot be permitted a role in the maintenance and promotion of regional disparity, by whatever device. The province of Saskatchewan has the most unfavourable transport position of the three prairie provinces, both from an import and export point of view. Our closest port is Churchill, at present limited to an 85 day season. Our main domestic markets for potash, pulp and lumber are in the mid west United States, a long all rail haul. Because of our central, land locked geographical location, our weak truck competition, and because the railways have been given the freedom under the National Transportation Act of 1967 to vary rates without reference to the regulatory authority, Saskatchewan makes the highest contributions to rail overhead costs on all rates, except export grain, of any province in Canada.
The railways perform certain services in the public interest for which they are paid subsidies. Since the passage of the National Transportation Act, some $410 million has been paid to the railways to the end of 1971. In addition, freight rates have been increased anywhere from 29 per cent to 67 per cent. In the intervening period, the railways have been confronted with enlarged export movements of coal, potash and grain. In fact, the railways have been unable to cope with the demand for certain freight services because of equipment shortages. Thus, potash sales go by the board because we cannot move it in sufficient quantities to Vancouver, and the federal government has to purchase 2,000 hopper cars for grain.
This brings me to a discussion of the National Transportation Act and some of the consequences of the removal of regulations in the railway system. The nub of the National Transportation Act of 1967 is expressed as follows:
Regulation of all modes of transport will not be of such a nature as to restrict the ability of any mode of transport to compete freely with any other mode of transport.
Released from regulation of rates, except when the Canadian Transport Commission might be asked by a shipper to review a rate, the railways have adopted an almost automatic formula for rate increases-one in the spring and one in the fall-without having to account to any regulatory tribunal. Since 1967 the general freight rate level has increased, as I have stated, from 29 per cent to 67 per cent depending on whether or not the rates are between eastern and western Canada or within western Canada.
April 16, 1973

The reason we in western Canada are suffering a 67 per cent maximum increase in rates can be understood more readily if we examine the following figures relating to the province of Ontario. It has been estimated that in Ontario 65 per cent of all freight loaded is transported by truck, including well over 80 per cent of all manufactured goods. No such comparable situation exists in western Canada, and particularly in Saskatchewan. In Ontario and Quebec, competition has acted as a brake to increasing transport costs. In the west, longer distances, small plants and low production volume of secondary industry, sparse population, plus a dependence on primary agriculture and resource industry, have militated against a breakdown of the rail monopoly and we pay the penalty in higher rates.
What can we do about excessive freight rates? As I have mentioned in my brief summary, a shipper can appeal to the Canadian Transport Commission to review a freight rate if the rate seems "to prejudicially affect the public interest". If the shipper makes a prima facie case to the commission, the commission will hold hearings and conduct an investigation. The rapeseed crushers of Western Canada and the Prince Albert Pulp Co. are cases in point. In fact, they are the first major cases placed before the commission since the new act was put on the statute books.
The rapeseed hearings lasted five weeks in Saskatoon, plus additional hearings in Ottawa. Legal counsel represented the three prairie governments, the governments of Ontario and Quebec, the eastern and western crushers and the railways. The total cost will run into hundreds of thousands of dollars. Without the support of our three provincial governments, the rapeseed crushers could not have processed their legitimate case. The Prince Albert Pulp Co., seeking reductions in rates into the United States, had to proceed before the interstate commerce commission in the United States as well as the Canadian Transport Commission. Here, too the total costs will be in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. You can see that only large companies or governments can successfully cope with appeals against unjust freight rates at the present time. The dice are loaded in favour of the railways in so far as the average shipper is concerned and unequalhanded justice is dispensed from Montreal or Winnipeg.
I submit that the Canadian Transport Commission has shown, to date, a pro-rail bias. I had hoped that when Mr. Pickersgill retired, a person familiar with regional transport problems would be appointed chairman. In fact, representations to the federal government to this effect were made by western Canadian provincial governments. What happened? We got Mr. Benson. I do not want to prejudge the new chairman but we from the west, and people in the Atlantic provinces as well, are sick and tired of having our vital problems of transportation decided finally by retired Ontario politicians. We demand that amendments be made to the National Transportation Act to simplify appeals against unjust rates so that the average shipper has access to the commission. We want a bridle to be put on the seemingly insatiable demands of the railways for high rates. We want the railways to maintain an adequate level of service to western Canadian communities.
CNR and Air Canada
What is required, Mr. Speaker, in western Canada and in Saskatchewan specifically, is a national transportation policy which is directed toward regional development. Instead of milking the west and keeping it as a source of raw material, a determined regional and national effort must be made to broaden our industrial base. When present transportation policy is a deterrent, as it now is, that policy must be changed. We must use our transportation policy as a vehicle of regional development.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the hon. members who have spoken on this important subject this afternoon, and I am surprised that once again government members are not interested in what is happening with respect to the financing of Canadian National Railways and Air Canada. Apparently they believe that we should pass this item and proceed to another order of business. If this matter is not important, then obviously there is really not any point in discussing it.
I note that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Comtois) is here, but really this is a transportation matter and concerns something that has been the cause of a lot of problems to a lot of people over an extended period of time. A great deal of it centres around the financing of the railway. I have been glancing over some of the figures, and really nothing has changed. The last financial statement I have for the Canadian National is the annual report for 1971. All one needs to do is to read the general survey of the report. It shows gross revenues less non-rail revenues at $135 million. It shows operating revenues of $1,148.8 million, and expenses of $1,119.5 million. Net railway operating income was $21.3 million, other income $22.9 million, and net income before interest on debt $44.2 million. Net interest on debts totalled $68.5 million. That is the crux of the problem, Mr. Speaker. Are we going to be stupid enough to allow the government to continue something that has been recognized by most Members of Parliament for years as being in itself completely stupid? Or are we going to change the situation?
In the last parliament most of us decided that we would not pass the next financing bill of the Canadian National. So, an election took place. That situation does not exist now. I would like to know from the government how the hell it got around that situation. It has an obligation to tell us. What kind of tool did it use to do something it was not able to do in parliament? Did it use treasury bills to finance the Canadian National capitalization debt? Or did it just let the debt accumulate? It may seem as if this bill is a small item. My arithmetic is not good, but I have added up the figures and they come to approximately $486 million for the Canadian National and $270 million for Air Canada, which is about half a billion dollars for CN and a quarter of a billion dollars for Air Canada. To a Liberal government, the way it plays around with figures, that is not a sizeable amount of money, but we have not been given an explanation of what happened to the debt last year. It came to a total of $70 million. We did not pay that.
The reason that I and other members are interested in this is that the Canadian people have been told that they own the Canadian National, ever since the days of the Grand Trunk and the other railways that went broke.

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
That happened long before my time. But, Mr. Speaker, we have never paid for it. It is like buying an automobile and never becoming the owner of it. You pay the interest on the debt, and eventually the automobile wears out, so that you end up not owning anything. We still do not own anything in so far as the capital debt of the Canadian National is concerned. One does not have to go through the whole financial report to understand this. Most members are not competent to understand the financial report, and I confess to being one of them, although I have studied the CN report for a number of years and do know a small amount about it.
I know that in 1970 we paid $75.5 million as interest on debt, but before making that payment the railway had a net profit of $45.8 million. In effect, we have not reduced the debt at all. Some of that debt is owing to people who are long dead. Some of it carries an interest rate of 3 per cent in perpetuity. Bonds are still held by people in England and still carry an interest rate not unlike the previous one. This year the Canadian National Railways made a profit of $44.2 million, so it could have bought the hopper cars or established some branch lines or put a line into the Arctic if that were desirable. However, it could do none of those things because this year we have payment on the debt of $68 lA million. In times of war or other times when we find that we cannot pay off the principal of the bonds we put that amount into the national debt and pay out of national revenues the amount necessary to carry that debt. The debt is to buy the railway, not to operate it. Is it not time that we decided to write off the debt so that we can look at what the railway is supposed to be doing?
This bill indicates that the loan to Air Canada will be limited to $1 billion. We are going to lend Canadian National $270 million, but this gets mixed up with what was originally the capital for the purchase of the railway and what is normal operating expenses. An examination of the financial structure will show who owns the shares in Canadian National Railways, and the exact interest rates being paid, but there is a division between capital expenditures being made for current operating purposes and the capitalization originally provided to buy the railway on which we pay this huge amount of interest.
Some hon. members have mentioned problems in their particular areas. In my riding of Timiskaming there is the wholly owned Northern Ontario Railway, the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Most of us know that the railways are not operating to the advantage of many areas in this country. They are not .doing the job they should in theMaritimes or in northern Ontario. In fact, I believe they are not doing the job that they should in any part of Canada.
I was amused by a question which was asked today about amalgamating the services in Regina and Saskatoon. Many members from Ontario wonder what the improvement would be in the new service, and whether the service centres were going to eliminate the people working at the stations. Apparently a telephone service would enable you to order a boxcar or arrange for carload freight. It can all be done by a telephone call to the service centre. It has not worked to our advantage-the rates keep going up and the service keeps going down.

Yesterday I boarded a plane at six o'clock and arrived in Ottawa a little after eleven o'clock. That is the kind of service that is provided in northern Ontario. It would only have taken an extra two hours to drive the distance. Most of my travel is around Ontario. Years ago I used to be able to get on a train, go to bed, and wake up in any of the major cities of the country. The other day I ordered a bedroom and I found that it cost $28. What do I get for that? I am sure I am not interested in the porter-they do not even have stewardesses on the train. I am not sure what I get for the $28 except that I am getting rooked. The price of a bedroom is a disgrace when nothing has been added since it used to cost $12. The railways are pricing themselves out of the market.
The annual report mentions that Canadian National has applied for abandonment of most of the passenger services in Canada. This is not because they want to get out of the passenger business but because the CTC said that unless they make the application for abandonment they are not entitled to the 80 per cent subsidy the government will provide. Mr. Speaker, we can do something about putting the Canadian National Railways on a sound national basis. We can pay off that debt so that we know what the railway is making. The railway is making a profit of $44 million, but the interest payment on the capital debt is $68i million, leaving a deficit of $25 million. It seems to me that we must make some changes.
We have done some other foolish things in the area of transportation, Mr. Speaker. In this bill there is a reference to paying for an aircraft in sterling. Obviously, this would be one of the large superjets that we contemplated buying several years ago, the supersonic aircraft. No consideration has been given to building an airport for this type of aircraft which travels at three times the speed of sound. We have made no attempt to provide ground transportation to cope with such a modern society. We are still in the horse and buggy days-perhaps we have moved one step ahead, since we are no longer firing boilers with coal but have diesel engines now. However, that is all we have done. I am sure there is some Canadian National rolling stock still around which is steam driven and which has not been upgraded. I suggest that much of it is in the passenger service.
We are going to buy STOL aircraft to fly from Ottawa to Montreal. If we had a rapid transit system similar to the monorail in Japan which travels at speeds up to 300 miles an hour, it would be possible to travel from downtown Ottawa to downtown Montreal in one half the time required for STOL. There would be half the disadvantages of STOL. There would not be the dislocation of people and that sort of thing. We would not have to buck the traffic, nor would we have to drive on a speedway to the airport.
This is most amusing. In Ottawa, we built a speedway to the airport to facilitate traffic. We then allowed the National Capital Commission and the RCMP to use it as a source of revenue. In the city, the speed limit is 35 miles an hour and on the airport speedway, the limit is 30 miles an hour. Possibly the minister thinks that is a scenic drive and people will want to look around. I thought it was designed to speed up airport traffic, but that is not true. We drive faster in the city than on that blooming park-
April 16, 1973

way. That is the way we run our transportation system. Everything is backwards. This is what is happening in all fields of transportation. We have not faced the major problems. We have not faced the problem of financing the railway. Until we solve our major problems, many other problems will remain unsolved.
There may not be much support for building a railroad to the Prudhoe Bay area. It may not be possible to haul gas and oil by tankcars. It may not be possible to build a line along the west shore of Hudson Bay into the high Arctic. It may not be possible to extend the railway from Pine Point to the Arctic. History will show that this is by far the most advantageous way of opening our north.
I know something about northern rail lines. There is one in northern Ontario which was built through 100 miles of muskeg. If you got off the ballast track there, you would have difficulty walking. This line goes through many miles of low land before reaching Moosonee, but it has not disrupted the ecology of the area. It is a year-round facility that meets the needs of that area and, in my opinion, it should be expanded to meet other needs. I am not suggesting the CNR should have three or four lines into the high Arctic. However, we should be considering a railway line into this area. Already there is talk about using air tankers to bring oil to Montreal. We should be considering a ground facility. However, the general public would not support such a proposal as long as we do not have the brains to eliminate the financing problem that has been carried on for almost 100 years since we bought the bankrupt railways at an exorbitant price. We have never been in a position to pay off the principal. We are still trying to carry the interest.
We should look at this financing bill in a realistic way. The government should have enough gumption to tell us how the problem was solved last year. If the government does not need parliament to pass this bill, then let us move on to another order of business. It the government is really interested in the development of transportation, they should be honest enough to tell us what is being financed. Does the government intend to use this money to give a 3 per cent or 4 per cent cost of living increase to the widows of those who retired from the CNR many years ago? Do they intend to increase the pension of retired railroad workers? Do they intend to purchase new equipment or are they going to continue to pay the debt under the guise of other methods of financing? Obviously, the government has used other methods in the past. Last year parliament did not pay $75 million. This must have been paid in some other way or added on to something else. Before considering this bill, we need answers to some of these serious questions.
I have often said that we in this party are not interested in maintaining a second Senate, the Canadian Transport Commission. This Commission has been totally unsuccessful in handling the problems of the railways and other transportation problems. We have the idiotic situation where a second airport is being built outside of Toronto. Because one was built near Montreal, we must build one near Toronto. Because a white elephant was built at Ste Scholastique, we must build a white elephant at Pickering. Surely, there is more to this country than satisfying the idiosyncrasies of the people who live in Toronto and Mont-
CNR and Air Canada
real. If one city gets something, the other must have the same.
If the Canadian Transport Commission is going to do anything, it will have to solve some of these idiotic problems. Parliament should make the commission deal with some of the problems which face individual Members of Parliament. The transportation system is not satisfactory in any part of Canada. All kinds of deals have been made over the years that no longer apply. Many concessions that were made are no longer applicable. If some of these problems were solved, it would help the disadvantaged areas of this country. Whenever I attend a meeting in northern Canada or the Maritimes, I am always informed that it is the transportation problems that retard development. If that is true, every member who represents those areas should violently object to the passage of this bill until the government tells us what the transportation policy of this country is.
Although there are only slightly more than 20 million people in this country, we have two international airlines, plus the charter airlines. It was decided that CP should service one half this country and Air Canada the other. Any reasonable government would amalgamate these two airlines. There are reasons for not amalgamating the railways. They have been around a long time. They have built-in peculiarities, and have been given all kinds of benefits. There may not be any equality in rail transportation unless we take the whole Canadian Pacific and the whole Canadian National and unite them. But that is not true of Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Airlines. This is the only country to my knowledge which allows itself the luxury of two international airlines, one going to the east and one going to the west. If Mr. Pratt has guts enough to stand up to the government it will be a surprise to me because he has never done so before. I congratulate him and I hope he wins in his fight to see that Air Canada goes into Italy. Why not? This area does not appear to me to be in Asia or the far east. It appears, to me, to be close to Central Europe. If the old agreement were in force, Air Canada'would have control of all the developments in the western area.
We should amalgamate those two air services. They should be considered as one agency, an agency of which Canadians should be proud and which they could use to make travel arrangements whether they were going east or west. We could call it whatever we liked. One of the largest airlines in the world is BOAC. Just a few months ago it amalgamated with its domestic counterpart. These companies, in England, were handling overseas, domestic and charter business. The decision has now been taken to amalgamate for the sake of efficiency, and I believe this decision meets with the approval of most people around the world who have become accustomed to using BOAC and identifying it with Britain.
You know, Mr. Speaker, I am not opposed to Canadian Pacific. If Canadian Pacific wants to take over Air Canada I would probably not have much objection. However, I think it is idiotic to allow these two large airlines, one in the east and one in the west, to operate as national airlines when we are such a small population in such a large area, and when so little service is provided in certain areas. I am

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
sure that even some of those who would not like to see Canadian Pacific taken over would agree that we in Canada are not getting service in feeder line areas. A while ago we decided to give northern Ontario to Nordair. Nordair does not want it. Nordair wants the line into Toronto because it is a paying proposition. But they don't want to go into northern Ontario. They don't want to go into Val d'Or. They don't want to go to Rouyn. They don't want to go to Timmins. They don't want to go to Sudbury. They want to fly from Montreal to Toronto.
If Air Canada had all the air routes in Canada, I am sure that what they lost on the apples they would make up on the oranges. They could run the overseas flights and they could run the trans-Canada flights-yes, and they could run flights into the areas represented by the hon. members to my right and give them better service to the main distribution points. I am sure that since it is a northern riding the minister is aware of many places from which people find it difficult to find scheduled flights to the north or south. That is true all across this country.
I am, personally, of the opinion that first things should come first.

Most members of the House in the last parliament were agreeable to the proposition that the first thing to be done involved the financing of the Canadian National Railways. Then, we would decide what was to be done about the company's capital structure. There is no question that Canadian National will need to borrow money. But any money borrowed to expand the railway should be money that the company is capable of repaying. But when we saddled the company with a debt which the company inherited when it came into being,-and, remember, it is parliament which always picks up the interest on this debt-it occurs to me that we did not buy this service; we just borrowed it from somebody and are just keeping up the payments. It is high time we did something about this situation.
Mr. Speaker, the government does not appear to be interested. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is not here. I do not know whether the parliamentary secretary is here or not.

speechtext:
Well, he may have to travel back here by rail and in that case we may not see him until after Easter. If he does travel by rail, he will be doing his job. I am sure most Members of Parliament have not been on a train for years and years. I am sure the Minister of Transport has not been on a train for years. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre has just disillusioned me by saying the parliamentary secretary was here earlier in the day and that he is therefore unlikely to be traveling around in the train finding out about the system.

What I am saying, though, is that there does not appear to be much interest in the subject we are discussing. Yet it is an important subject. I am of the opinion that Canada has not outgrown the railways, that there is a need in this country today for railways and that this need will continue for a long time to come. In particular, those who come from northern areas are well aware that when an area is developed by railroad there is a permanency to the development which cannot be brought about in any other way. It has certainly not been achieved by highway development. I believe this is true of the developments in Labrador, of the developments in Newfoundland, of the developments in northern Ontario and other regions.
It is interesting to note that northern Ontario developed and became a recognizable area only when the government of Ontario was forced to build the Colonial Railroad. When they did so silver and cobalt were found, and that is how Toronto was born. Before that, there were cabbage towns with few people and little money. After the railroad went into northern Ontario, nickel was found in Sudbury, gold was found in Kirkland Lake and Timmins, copper was found in the area and for years we supported the people of Toronto out of these resources. All this came about as a result of the Ontario Northland Railway. I am sure this is equally true of the developments in western Canada, of the developments in the Northwest Territories, in the uranium field at Pine Point and I am sure it is true of the development in Wabush. Lake St. John, I am sure, has a similar story to tell and I suggest there will be other sagas of railroading to be written in days to come about extension into the high Arctic in the centre, in the east and through the Yukon. They will make very interesting reading. They will make much better reading if we take from around the neck of the Canadian National the debt we hung there a hundred years ago, make it part of the national debt and make the interest payment direct from the treasury.
Obviously, this is a debt which the railway company cannot pay, one which it will never be able to pay, and one which is now being compoundied through bills of the kind before us which ask for specific amounts of money, in this particular case half a billion dollars, which appears to be required for capital expenditure. According to financial statements of the past, the company has been able to undertake capital expenditures in the past from its own funds after allowing for depreciation, the writing off of assets, and so on. But the railway has never been able to write off the debt which it inherited when the company was founded. In fact, the government has usually assumed the burden of the interest payments. It is true that in recent years the company made a payment of $25 million. Most of the money, however, comes out of general revenue, and it seems that this is the major problem we face.
The present government will, I am sure, make no change in transportation Policy. No change will be made for two reasons. First, the government will not admit that the Canadian Transport Commission which it devised, and which parliament established, and which I voted for because I thought it would serve an important purpose, has, in fact, failed to do the job for which it was set up. The Commission has failed to set any kind of reasonable policy. The CTC has also failed the general public in its approach to Bell Telephone and its tariff rates. It has
April 16, 1973

failed the general public with regard to making mandatory, service to the population in areas that need service. It has been used as a kind of Senate for retired politicians who did not want to return to their former practice, and has really met Dawson's requirements for politics in Canada that there must always be a body to which politicians who have served their usefulness can retire without getting into any difficulty.

Why does the government not look in the mirror and ask itself why it has not proclaimed Part III of the National Transportation Act? Why has it not got around the proclaiming what, in effect, was to be the guts of the National Transportation Act? I was one of those who supported the legislation. We did not set up the Canadian Transport Commission just to be an agency for retired politicians, or to decide whether Bell should get another five cents on its telephone bills, or whether it was just and reasonable that people in remote areas should have rail transporation available to them. The commission has the necessary expertise and we gave them legislation which allowed for greater leeway than most other agencies have been allowed. Yet it has failed totally. In fact, problems have got worse rather than better. I suggest-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-164, I want to say at the outset that I concur with a number of the remarks which were made by my hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), particularly with his reference to the failure of the government to implement Part III of the National Transportation Act which, in essence, constitutes the spirit of that legislation. I also concur with his remarks in respect of the manoevring and manipulation that have taken place in regard to Bill C-4, the previous CNR financing bill which died on the order paper in the last parliament, and the introduction of this particular piece of legislation.
I believe it is rather disturbing that, after a lapse of more than a year, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has now introduced Bill C-164 to cover the financial operations of Air Canada and the CNR for the period January 1, 1973 to June 30, 1974, and then implies through his parliamentary secretary that it should be disposed of without
CNR and Air Canada
delay. The previous bill Bill C-4, covered the operations of the CNR and Air Canada for the period January 1, 1971 to June 30, 1972. As hon. members know, it was never ratified by parliament. It was not even submitted to committee for study. As a result, a number of questions arise. I suggest that this bill should not be proceeded with or sent to committee until some of the questions that arise have been answered.
The first question is this. If Bill C-4 was to have been the vehicle providing for the authorization of certain sums of money to meet capital requirements for the operations of Air Canada and the CNR for the period January 1, 1972 to June 30, 1972, how was the business of Air Canada and the CNR transacted during this period without the ratification of parliament? Or is this bill simply a "nothing" matter which is used as a piece of filler legislation?
The second question is this. Inasmuch as Bill C-4 covered the period from January 1, 1971 to June 30, 1972 and Bill C-164, the bill we are now dealing with, covers the period January 1, 1973 to June 30, 1974, what has happened in regard to the six-month period of July 1, 1972 to December 31, 1972? Were no moneys expended during this period, or is there some other form of interim financing of carte blanche approval granted which in effect nullifies the necessity for these bills being presented annually? I suggest that this indeed is a very frustrating exercise and a questionable manoeuvre. Surely, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) should explain their actions in this regard.
We all are all frequently reminded of the days when this government had a huge majority which on many occasions it exercised to circumvent the will of parliament. We experienced the failure of the government to pay necessary sums under the provisions of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and also the difficulties with the Unemployment Insurance Act. Therefore, we ask ourselves whether this is simply another example of the type of arrogance that has been displayed in past days. I ask the government what held it back from proceeding with this measure in the last parliament. It had a huge majority and certainly had ample time to bring the bill forward and push it through committee.
As near as I can determine-I stand to be corrected since I am not a legal expert, a lawyer, or an authority on the operations of the Financial Administration Act or the CNR financing act-it appears to me very clear that the government has circumvented the role of parliament and acted in a manner which, in my opinion, is contrary to the provisions of the CNR act and the Financial Administration Act. If there is a legal loophole in this connection, I believe that one of the ministers of the Crown owes it to the House to explain what the loophole is; then, and only then, can we judge the importance of and the priority that should be given to this bill.
A third question arises, Mr. Speaker, and that is the question of the appointment of auditors, a matter alluded to by members who have spoken before me. Bill C-4 provided for the appointment of new auditors. However, as a result of that bill not being ratified to we have that section in this bill. Section 38 of the Canadian National Railways Act reads:

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
A continuous audit of the accounts of National Railways shall be made by independent auditors appointed annually by Parliament who shall annually report to Parliament in respect of their audit.
I simply want to ask what firm is now doing the auditing for the CNR and Air Canada. Are they being paid and, if so, under what authority? The parliamentary secretary offered an explanation in his submission when introducing the bill in the House last Friday. He pointed out that the auditing would be done on a rotating basis, and also that the rotating auditors would be appointed for a five to six year term. This would probably be an acceptable compromise.
No mention was made in Bill C-4 of the possibility of rotating auditors; there was simply a section dealing with the appointment of a new firm of auditors, namely the firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell and Company, a change from the traditional group of Touche, Ross and Co. There was no explanation as to why the change was being implemented. Of course, parliament never really had the opportunity to deal with the matter in any great detail. I would simply ask whether this was a decision taken unilaterally by the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Benson, and was it a reward for services rendered in past years to the firm of Peat, Marwick & Mitchell. We all know that the government looks after its friends and that it also looks after its defeated candidates. I am wondering what the government is trying to hide.
