speechtext:
If everything is above board, Mr. Speaker, why has the government failed to produce the documents to which I have referred in notice of motion for papers No. 77 which reads:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of all correspondence, telegrams and other documents between the Minister of Finance and/or other responsible Ministers, and the auditing firms of Touche, Ross and Co., Peat, Marwick and Mitchell, in connection with the auditing services for Air Canada and Canadian National Railways.
This question has remained on the order paper since January, 1973, yet to this date I have received no reply, nor have I received the documentation in question. I simply ask what the government is trying to hide and what is going on here.
I should like to know why the 1972 budget for Canadian National was not tabled in this House until Thursday, February 8, 1973. If that is a normal occurrence, I suppose the government can offer that explanation. I simply ask in all sincerity why there was that kind of a delay, and why we have not had either an audited statement in respect of the CNR and Air Canada for 1972 or the annual reports. Is this because we do not have a firm of auditors ratified by parliament which could provide an audited statement and an annual report? What happens if parliament, in its wisdom, decides not to approve Clause 14 of Bill C-164, which provides for the appointment of two auditing firms? In view of the type of explanation we have been getting in respect of this particular facet of the bill, parliament may not see fit to pass this clause. Let me reiterate the fact that

under the provisions of Bill C-4 there was simply a change in the firm of auditors to be appointed.
When the parliamentary secretary introduced this bill he said, as reported at page 3297 of Hansard for April 13:
If the policy of rotating auditors were adopted, we should have to study carefully the frequency of the rotation. Evidently, the duration of the assignment should not be too short, because, otherwise, the auditors would hardly have enough time to familiarize themselves with the operations of the company and the intricacies of its accounting system, not to mention the special accounting requirements of the Canadian Transport Commission.
On the other hand, the long-term appointments made in the past covered far too long periods. Consequently, it was agreed that a five to six years' appointment would be an acceptable compromise, the first year and the last year to be overlapping periods during which two auditing firms would be hired.
Under Clause 14 of Bill C-164 we find that the firm of Peat, Marwick and Mitchell will be the auditors for the year which has concluded, 1972, and for the year 1973 we have the firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell and Company and the firm of Coopers & Lybrand, both of the cities of Toronto and Montreal. For the year 1974, we will have the firm of Coopers & Lybrand. Those facts do not coincide with the policy enunciated by the parliamentary secretary. I should like to know if this is a makeshift change which came about as a result of an embarrassing situation which the government found itself in, or is this simply a form of corruption?
An hon Member: It is Liberal corruption.

speechtext:
Those are some of the questions in respect of which I believe this House requires an explanation. In my opinion, if these financing bills have any legal connotation whatever, then no firm of auditors, whether it be Touche, Ross and Co. or Peat, Marwick and Mitchell, have the authority to carry out the auditing services for the CNR and Air Canada. That being the case, I would ask the appropriate ministers of the Crown to explain this situation. Is this simply another example of this government's arrogance and inability to bring forward its legislation in an orderly manner? Whatever the answer, we should have some explanation.
Let me now turn to the nitty-gritty of the bill, and deal first with the operations of Air Canada and CNR. It should be clearly established that these two organizations form a vital and integral part of our transportation network in this country, and provide as suggested in Section 3 of the National Transportation Act:
-and economic efficient and adequate transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest total cost is essential to protect the interests of the users of transportation and to maintain the economic well-being and growth of Canada, and that these objectives are most likely to be achieved when all modes of transport are able to compete under conditions ensuring that having due regard to national policy and to legal and constitutional requirements-
When examining the operations of the CNR and Air Canada, I believe we must examine their performance in the light of this statutory statement of policy. There is no question in my mind, nor I am sure in the minds of hon. members in this House, that air transportation is a vitally important aspect of the development of Canada with its problems in respect of distance, sparse population and the development of various regions including the north.
April 16, 1973

At the present time it is interesting to note the game that is taking place between the Chairman of Air Canada and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). Much has been said in the House and in the press about the desirability of cutting up the aviation pie, as it has been referred to by my friends to the left. We should be under no illusions in this House that the Chairman of Air Canada is anything but one of the government's boys. I am sure that during his numerous discussions with the Minister of Transport, to which he has alluded on a number of occasions, everything has been rosy. I am sure they are dedicated to the same purposes and principles. I do not believe there is any conflict between the two.
The chairman of Air Canada is concerned about profit and protection. He believes competition is bad. Well, one can wonder how much less competition he really wants. After all Air Canada controls 75 per cent of Canadian air passenger service while Canadian Pacific Air Lines gets 25 per cent. Therefore, the growth of Canadian Pacific Air Lines and its penetration is predicated upon the growth and penetration of Air Canada. So, why the concern? Whatever Air Canada's competition may be, it will never exceed more than 25 per cent of the Canadian market because of the present policy. As a businessman this is very difficult for me, and I am sure for anyone who has ever been in business, to understand, especially in view of the remarks of the chairman of Air Canada who suggests that competition is bad for business. He suggests it is bad for the customer and bad for the company. This is particularly difficult to understand in view of the fact that Air Canada is assured of a 75-25 per cent allocation of the market.
I believe basic business principles apply equally to big business and small business. I sincerely believe competition is the lifeblood of business. In my opinion, it creates innovation and attracts technological advancement. I believe competition can provide a higher standard of service for the customer, in this case the travelling public. I believe customer satisfaction is a key to profit. I submit that the chairman of Air Canada, rather than running around in an effort to generate a certain amount of sympathy for Air Canada, would do better to examine his organization and direct his effort toward improving the service. He should be broadening airline service to more Canadians in this country. I also believe that competition can serve to reduce waste and inefficiency. If waste and inefficiency were reduced, this also would be beneficial to the customer and indeed to the corporation. Moreover, competition can create a challenge which in turn would help improve harmony and morale within the organization. This is something which obviously is lacking in the general structure of Air Canada.
I think competition creates a desire, if you are number one, to remain number one or if you are number two to try harder because you are aware that there is someone else knocking on the door. If a person has any dedication or loyalty to the company for which he is working, he will try harder if the company should be in the top spot to retain that position or if it should be in the second spot he will try harder to get it to the top. I think this is a situation which places everyone on their toes. It creates a
CNR and Air Canada
climate in which people pull together in an effort to do the job and serve the public. This is what Air Canada should be directing itself toward.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED TRANSFER OF LAND AND BUILDINGS AT CANADIAN FORCES STATION LADNER TO MUNICIPALITY OF DELTA, BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of transferring the Crown lands, commonly known as the Canadian Forces Station Ladner or the Old Boundary Bay Airport, together with the buildings thereon, to the municipality of Delta and, in co-operation with the municipality, develop the areas as an industrial-recreational complex of pollution-free secondary industries, parkland, ocean beaches and sports stadia for the benefit of Delta, Richmond and the Lower Mainland and as an example to other medium-sized urban and suburban communities of the value of such a complex.
He said: Mr. Speaker, possibly no greater opportunity exists for the government to contribute to the over-all development of an area with a minimum capital investment than in the Boundary Bay area of the municipality of Delta in British Columbia. In co-operation with the municipality of Delta, there exists an area with potential for development as an industrial-recreational complex comprised of pollution free secondary industry, parkland, ocean beaches, and sports facilities. This complex would benefit not only the residents of Delta and Richmond, but also the entire lower mainland of B.C. and could serve as an example to other medium-sized urban and suburban communities.
We have already seen the federal government propose multi-million dollar developments for the Toronto waterfront and we have an idea of the benefit that will be
accorded the citizens of the entire metropolis. We have seen how multi-million dollar expenditures on Montreal's Expo have served to benefit the citizens of Montreal by completely changing an area that previously offered very little. Benefits of similar proportion can be accomplished in the area to which I am referring with an investment of one fraction the amount of money. But the government must take positive steps now if these goals are to be achieved.
For example, at this particular site there is an airport hangar which at the present moment is of little value. With modifications, and again limited expenditure, this facility could be turned into an arena to serve the needs of the thousands of children and sports enthusiasts in one of the fastest growing areas in Canada. The miles of beaches that are presently not being used for recreational purposes could be transformed into one of the finest beach areas in the province with limited federal spending. In addition, the very real possibility exists of turning the entire Boundary Bay area into a vital tax resource for all levels of government. With limited government investment, the existing Boundary Bay airport could become the lower mainland's principal airport for small private aircraft in the years to come. The tendency over the past decade has been to segregate the larger aircraft from smaller aircraft used for business and utility purposes. One of the most costly items in the construction of any airport is in the initial acquisition of land, but in this case the land, with an existing airport, is already there. The principal cost now is in maintenance rather than in acquisition.
It would be in the best interests of all who carry on business from the Burnaby-Richmond-Delta and lower mainland area to have an active local airport for small private aircraft at this location. In addition, the advantages are obvious to those interested primarily in the recreational facilities which could be incorporated virtually hand in hand. New businesses would be attracted to the Delta area by virtue of the fact that they could locate near an airport which could effectively and efficiently carry personnel to their branch plants. The airport would thus aid in the growth of the area and offer greater employment opportunities in the entire mainland area.
New facilities will be necessary to support this industry and thus contribute to the over-all economy of the area. Possibly some of the smaller firms presently located at the Vancouver international airport will move due to the high lease rates and the overcrowding. This, in turn, will permit an orderly expansion of the present facilities at the Vancouver international airport. Boundary Bay airport is already built and is served by good access roads. There is no other area that is so capable of incorporating the airport, an industrial complex and a recreational complex all in one, each one nurturing the other, and each one complementing the other.
Possibly, the former Centralia air force base could be regarded as an example of an industrial development which became successful because of its airport. But no such undertaking can be successful without a proper environmental impact study carried out with respect to the implementation of this proposal. It is appreciated that an environmental impact study cannot be completed overnight, but the long-range program in this case is of such

April 16, 1973

importance and of such over-all benefit to the people concerned that virtually everyone is prepared to accept the fact that time is required. But what is most important is that the government consider this proposal, consider the advantages, consider the need for a recreational area, consider the need for additional job-creating light industry, consider the quickly disappearing waterfront recreational land available and commit itself to an in depth study with the minimum amount of delay. The corporation of Delta is prepared to assist in the establishment of a joint environmental study of the available facilities, and the council will render all possible assistance and co-operation to the federal authorities.
In conclusion, given the existing ingredients and the land availability, and given the spirit of co-operation among all levels of government as well as between ministerial offices, there is herein the opportunity not only to set an example in this field but to provide jobs through the creation of pollution free light industry and to afford a recreational facility for thousands of residents of the entire lower mainland. Mr. Speaker, I urge the government to consider and act upon this motion.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED TRANSFER OF LAND AND BUILDINGS AT CANADIAN FORCES STATION LADNER TO MUNICIPALITY OF DELTA, BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this motion, I should like to associate myself with the mover and seconder. I think it is a splendid idea that a motion such as this should be brought forth at this time, and hon. members should have an opportunity to debate it briefly on the floor of the House of Commons for it is my hope that we will see the motion sent to committee for study. I do not know the coastal part of B.C. as well as I know the interior where I have lived for many years but, having lived in the Vancouver district for a considerable period of time, I do know that the Boundary Bay area could be made into one of the outstanding environmental playgrounds on the Pacific coast. Having been a member of the B.C. legislature, I am aware of the fact that on numerous occasions over the years we have had briefs from various groups in the area urging that action be taken provincially to preserve many of the fine beaches to which the mover of the motion has referred.
A subject, in which all members are clearly interested and which was mentioned in the address we just heard, is the environmental studies. I urge the federal government to look into this part of the motion without delay. There is no reason why a sound environmental impact study could not be launched at this time, and I agree with the mover of the motion that it will take some time for an adequate study to be undertaken and for the results of that study to be assessed. We should not delay. Time is of the essence. The growing community of Vancouver and the whole Fraser valley area is in need of further recreational facilities, and here is an opportunity for the government to do something which would assist in setting this area aside for all time for the purposes outlined in the motion.
I know that it takes time for the wheels of government to get rolling and for the government take action. But again I am going to suggest to the government that they refer this motion to the appropriate committee for the necessary studies and I hope that it will pass the House of Commons this afternoon. Our group is certainly interested in seeing studies of this nature carried out, and we will
Transfer of Base at Ladner
certainly endorse the resolution which has been presented to the House this afternoon.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-164, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways System and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973, to the 30th day of June, 1974, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURE AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Prior to private members' hour, Mr. Speaker, I touched briefly on the matter of Air Canada and its policy of centralization, particularly in respect of the servicing and maintenance of aircraft. It seems to me that a number of questions arise as a result of this policy, particularly with the advent of the wide-bodies jets, the L-1011 and the 747. I believe these aircraft lay-over in the Vancouver area, and in my opinion it would make for a very efficient operation to carry out a certain amount of servicing and maintenance in Vancouver.
The other question is, what happens to the Dorval facilities when Ste. Scholastique goes into operation? There will be a certain amount of cost and inconvenience in ferrying aircraft from one airport to the other in order to carry out necessary maintenance. On the whole broad question one can only ask whether the concept of centralization has given the greater degree of efficiency in service and maintenance to Air Canada. Also, is the policy of centralization consistent with the policy of the federal government which has announced in many areas its attempt to decentralize operations.
I would be remiss if I failed to point out a matter which rather alarms me in the 1971 annual report of Air Canada. Are the huge costs of sales and promotion justified? Something in the order of $75.6 million was spent on sales and promotion to move 7.4 million passengers. That works out to $10 per passenger ticket. We might also ask whether Air Canada is utilizing these funds to take quarter-page ads in the Globe and Mail to push air traffic to Hawaii via Los Angeles through the Pan American system. We also wonder whether the administrative cost of $23.8 million, which works out to approximately $3 per passenger ticket, is justified. We question whether there could be any shaving of administrative expenditures, particularly in light of the fact that there are 19 or 20 vice-presidents on the Air Canada board of directors.
We also wonder about the desirability of the purchase of Wardair by Air Canada. It has been said that it was purchased because of its leadership in the charter field. But, Mr. Speaker, Air Canada controls 34 per cent of all charter traffic in Canada, while Wardair has roughly 27 per cent and Canadian Pacific approximately 10 per cent. In short, Air Canada handles more passengers on a summer weekend than Wardair does in a year, yet in putting its case before the Air Transport committee the argument was that Air Canada required a great amount of expertise in the movement of large numbers of people.
This argument seems to me invalid and I wonder what the real reason was for Air Canada's purchase of one-third of the interest of Wardair. Was it simply because the IDB has a huge investment in Wardair and the loan was to some extent in jeopardy? These are questions that must be answered, Mr. Speaker, because the argument put forth by Air Canada, namely, that it needed to acquire Wardair's expertise in the movement of large numbers of people, does not hold water in my opinion. On the broad picture we wonder whether this monopoly will bring about cheaper air fares for the travelling public, or will it breed more inefficiency and protection for Air Canada while in effect depriving passengers of freedom of choice?
I turn now to the matter of air service as it pertains to western Canada, particularly the cities of Edmonton and Calgary. I note with interest that Air Canada plans to expand its regional air service in northern Ontario. I have no argument with that because I realize it is important to have adequate air service in all parts of Canada. However, it seems to me rather inconsistent with Air Canada's policy, because over the years it has been attempting to get away from handling regional air traffic. It gave up the route between Calgary and Edmonton and left a void which was very successfully filled by Pacific Western Airlines.
I believe that Edmonton and Calgary deserve a direct link to the nation's capital; indeed, I believe that every provincial capital deserves a direct link to the nation's capital. What we in western Canada need is greater frequency of service. We do not necessarily need huge jets like the L-1011 and 747, but more DC-8 and DC-9 jets to connect with eastern and western Canada. We need more flights and additional international links with the United States.
Bilateral talks have been going on for some time. Edmonton is desirous of obtaining a link with Minneapo-lis-St. Paul. This has been talked out for years. The time has come when this service should become a reality. The advent of wide-bodied jets such as the L-1011 and the 747 will undoubtedly cut down further on our frequency of service. We do not want the frequency of service decreased. With these large jets, Air Canada will be more concerned about moving larger numbers of people rather than increasing service for these areas.
The cities of Calgary and Edmonton have grown and matured to the stage where they should have a direct link with Ottawa, rather than going through Toronto. There is quite a campaign going on in the city of Toronto about who wants airplanes flying around, and who does not. The

April 16, 1973

travelling public in western Canada who are heading to Ottawa would very much appreciate going around the bottleneck that exists at Toronto airport.
I want to summarize my presentation on air service by quoting from a study which was conducted by the Transportation and Development Authority of Calgary. The study is entitled "Air Service Requirements of Calgary, 1972-1976." I believe there are some valid points in this report. The report can be applied to many areas throughout Canada. I want to put this on record for consideration by the minister and others who are interested in the air transportation industry. I wish to quote from page 9 where the recommendation is as follows:
First, there is a growing tendency for regional carriers to assume responsibility for regional services, thus relieving Air Canada of that responsibility and weakening the agreement that Air Canada's financial position must be protected from serious transcontinental competition.
The next factor is something I pointed out earlier:
Second, there are numerous benefits to be realized from allowing competition. These include increases in frequency, quality, and efficiency. Third, the analyses upon which present restrictions were developed were conducted six years ago. Fourth, there is no certainty that the transcontinental market, given better service, would not be capable of supporting competition. Fifth, the present restrictions will not permit the gradual implementation of effective competition as the transcontinental markets expands.
These are good recommendations and should be considered when reviewing the over-all air transportation policy both in Canada and in respect of our international air service.
Throughout my presentation I may have sounded somewhat critical of the operations of Air Canada, but I want to say that I am very proud of Canada's national airline. There are a lot of dedicated people who work for that airline. However, I want to assure Your Honour that there has been a great deal of degeneration and deterioration in the service and, indeed, in the morale of the people who work for the airline.
The management should take a very close and hard look at their operations. I urge the chairman of Air Canada and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to stop playing this superficial game of cat-and-mouse and get on with the job of serving Canada's air travelling needs. They can encourage a greater degree of pride, initiative and dedication for the people who have worked so hard and have dedicated themselves to making Air Canada an efficient and proficient airline.
I want to deal briefly with the servocentre concept as it relates to Canadian National Railways. Much of what has been said about the implementation of the servocentre concept has been negative. I want to go on record as being totally against the concept of the servocentre. It is a sophisticated computer network. Canadian National have advised that the concept is not being initiated simply for economic reasons. If that is the case, we must ask for whose benefit the servocentre concept is being developed. Certainly it is not for the patrons of the railways.
Over the past number of years we have witnessed the closing of railway stations in smaller centres throughout western Canada. The business has not been funnelled to the larger centres. It has been lost. We do not have anything now to prove that it will be transferred to the larger
CNR and Air Canada
centres. When station operators are taken out of communities of 4,000 and 5,000 people, there is a drop in business accruing to the railways. There has been a great deal of centralization, with a number of smaller communities losing their station operators. The customers expect personalized service. They want a representative on hand, particularly with the degree of rationalization that has taken place to this date. How can anyone expect from a centralized computer center the kind of personal service he deserves? CN representatives say they will improve service by offering a Zenith telephone number and periodic visits by the customer representative. This has not worked in the past and it will not work now.
CN and CP are guilty of deliberately withdrawing from their responsibility of providing express service and passenger communications service to hundreds of small communities in Canada. I believe it is deliberate. If one looks at the stations now in existence, they see that they are the most run-down buildings in the communities. This is really disheartening, because to lose the CN or CP agent is to lose a very prominent citizen. He is one who has actively participated in the various activities of the community. To lose an on-hand representative is certainly very discouraging.
An application for a servocentre concept has been made in my community of Vegreville. Upon examining the revenues derived from that particular station, we found that one-third of the revenue generated was derived from passenger sales, express and communications services. One-third of all the revenue from that station comes from this source. I believe the CN should have an on-hand representative to properly look after this business and promote additional services.
In view of the fact the minister and the government have undertaken to examine the transportation needs and the economic opportunities of western Canada over the next year or so, I recommend that while this review is going on there should be an indefinite postponement of any further abandonment of station operators and the closing of these facilities. We cannot allow this to continue without having some knowledge of what the future holds with regard to the total transportation picture and the matter of rail line abandonment. We now have a number of studies which relate to the abandonment of a number of lines and elevators. This will ultimately result in reducing the number of elevators and the number of serviceable lines by approximately one-third. I urge the minister and this government to use their good offices to encourage CNR to stop this deliberate degredation of rural Canada. I see my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURE AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since Friday, I have been carefully listening to my hon. friends' speeches and unlike most of them, I do not feel compelled to use all my time, because I intend to clearly state my views instead of hearing myself talking and putting hon. members to sleep.
We are now studying Bill C-164, an act to authorize the provision of moneys for two Crown corporations. As it is asked by the government, we have to approve capital expenditures for the CNR and Air Canada.

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
Through the Governor General's recommendation we can evaluate that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is requesting an aggregate amount of $225,500,000 for the capital expenditures of the CN in 1973, $75 millions for the capital expenditures for the six first months of 1974, $167,500,000 to enter into contracts for new equipment, and finally, $21 millions for branch lines loans, and I do not know whether those $21 millions will be used by officials to branch out or only to take root in a foolish administration. Mr. Speaker, we are asked to approve $489 millions to maintain a business which is poorly run, without convenient service, which is 25 years behind and to perpetuate a stupid administration.
We heard Western members-conservative members because there are no liberals in those areas-members from Central provinces and Eastern Canada, and all of us have explained with numerous examples how rotten the present service is, the decrease in passenger service and the incompetency of CN officials.
Mr. Speaker, considering the way in which the government manages that type of undertaking, we wonder whether the people in charge of the CN are even slightly competent. It may even be that they are so incompetent as to be unable to carve out a peg to plug up a hole.
Mr. Speaker, this company is said to be responsible to Parliament. It is quite willing to ask for credit, but what control does the government exercise over it? None whatsoever, to the extent that towards the end of the recommendation in the bill, it is said, and I quote:
. .. such loans to be repaid from revenues of the Railway Company and Air Canada or . . .
And here go the government controls-
. .. or, if revenues prove insufficient by subsequent deficit appropriation by Parliament.
In other words, the government guarantees $489 million today, and if that proves insufficient it will give more. The government could not care less how it is spent, whether it is thrown out the window, spent on bubble gum, or what have you. It gives $489 million today and if in six months or a year from now that proves not to be enough, it will give more without exercising any control. Let it be spent on anything at all, or even thrown out the window, for that matter. And if you are short of money, we government idiots will give you more to replenish this $489 million petty cash.
Mr. Speaker, I shall say like one of my friends that this is not disgusting, it is damned disgusting to see such an administration. And through the Canadian Transport Commission, we try at a certain time to get justice. And what about these jerks who go beyond limits, beyond the government's authority, even Parliament's? These are arrogant officials like this chap, Thompson, who tells us stupidly: When I say no, it is no.
Here is proof that these corporations are in no way under government authority. They are only playing the hypocritical game of a mitigated democracy. These officials say: To hell with you. And I would not be surprised if they used the picturesque language of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to tell us to eat something.

Is it known that officials like those of the CNR and even of the government, delight in managing in the most "honourable" jumble.
Let us think about it. The CNR makes $42 million in profits but the interest on the debt amounts to $68 million. Finally, it reports at the end of the year a $20 million deficit. That is the management of a company that we cannot control. What progress has the CNR made? What modern method of transportation has it adopted? What did the government do to force it to improve its means of transportation? Absolutely nothing. Now, Canada developed according to the rythm of the railways at the turn of the century. Nowadays, means of transportation are still the same as they were at the beginning of the century. They do not want to create or improve the systems, they will delay their development.
This afternoon, we heard members from all sides of the House say it is badly operated. The CN does not want to improve the transportation systems while it is so important nowadays for example to consider more and more the needs to curb pollution. The government does not do anything to force these companies to improve their systems of transportation while complying with scientific data. Before approving moneys, why does the government not force these companies to allocate a fraction of the moneys to the improvement of means of transportation? Canada is the ideal country for that: Why not force the companies such as the CNR for example, to use faster trains? They do exist. Everyone has heard about them. In Japan, for instance, trains travel at 200 miles an hour which would be ideal for Canada, because of the distances involved. It would even solve the problems of requirements for increasingly larger airports, such as Pickering, or Sainte-Scholastique, and the resulting problems facing the people. Fast trains would be an ideal solution for travel from one city to another. Why does not the government compel the CNR to work in that direction? It does nothing about it.
We still pass the time voting funds and assuring the CNR that if it does not get that money, it will get some through special warrants. We have heard about the service provided to passengers on the Ottawa-Quebec, Quebec-Montreal or Montreal-Lake St. John lines or to people who travel on those 1890 cattle cars where no attention is given to passengers. However, on the Ottawa-Montreal line, there is an hourly bus service. Why could we not offer the same services through rapid train systems? No, we are satisfied with old systems which are kept going through legislation authorizing the granting of funds without compelling the recipients to do some development.
Such are the comments which I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker. My remarks relate not only to the transport system as such but also to its financing. As I said earlier, interest is up to $68 million and profits up to $42 million, so the deficit is down to $20 million. That is exactly the type of administration that we deplore and to which we are opposed.
The same thing happens at the government level where there exists a deficit system due to interest. We see the government decry inflation. Inflation is eating away at us.
April 16, 1973

The expenses of such crazy systems where you pay more interests then you can make profits are precisely a cause of inflation. When interests will have eaten away more of the profits of a company like the CN or the government it will be realized that inflation is still growing without being able to solve the problem.
We say that any new production must be financed through new credits and as long as the government does not admit that we will be caught in crazy systems such as those we have now, deficit systems, systems where prices steadily go up while quality goes down, where prices go up while easier access to consumer goods is being destroyed. Interest goes up, costs go up in such systems.
Creditists have said and repeated for many years that any new production must be financed through new credits and not through crazy loans to pay interests on fictitious debts as can now be seen with respect to the CN. As long as the government does not understand that, as long as it does not accept to consider in a positive way the suggestions we make, as long as we are presented with small bills such as the one before us to try and make us believe that the government is deciding more or less what decisions are to be taken by Crown corporations-because, in fine print, they are promised money by the barrel-we shall never see the end of it.
Mr. Speaker, those are the remarks I wanted to make and I hope that the government will wake up once and for all and acknowledge with us that the present system is debt oriented and not tailored to efficient service. It is about time to ensure that this objective is reached.

Mr. Speaker, in dealing with BillC-164,1 want to make it abundantly clear at the outset, as I have in the past, that I am not prepared to use Canadian National Railways as a whipping-boy. Nor am I in any way condemning the employees of the CNR. These are hard working, conscientious men and women dedicated to their task. Any criticism of transportation in Canada belongs at the door of this government, and particularly the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). Canadian National Railways and Air Canada are operators. They carry out the policy, or lack thereof, to the best of their ability. Where this policy is outdated or completely lacking, we cannot possibly blame the operators for the deplorable situation in which we find ourselves.
Railways are the backbone of this country, both literally and figuratively. Properly operated, Canadian National Railways has, in my opinion, a far greater potential for the reduction of regional disparity in this country than the Department of Regional Economic Expansion or any other program developed by this government. The key words are "properly operated". The present administration has not, to date, demonstrated any ability or inclination to bring in any policies consistent with the present needs, never mind the future; instead, they use exactly the same indifferent and arrogant approach that they have used in the past.
For the moment, let us consider the recent financing bills of the Canadian National Railways starting with Bill C-186, which was passed in 1971, covering the financing of the railway system and Air Canada from January 1, 1970, to June 30, 1971. Bill C-4, which was never passed, was
CNR and Air Canada
intended to cover the financing from January 1, 1971, to the first day of June, 1972. Then there was an overlap of six months, and finally we have Bill C-164, which covers from January 1, 1973, to June 30, 1974, leaving a gap of six months completely devoid of covering legislation. Was this overlap and gap of six months an error? Did the people in the department who prepare the legislation not know or not care? In any event, the whole time period was left without covering legislation and I will be interested in finding out in detail how this was and is to be handled.
We have the further irony of changing auditors after having accepted the seemingly satisfactory services of one company for many years. The change of auditors was announced in Bill C-4, which was of course, as I have said, never passed; and in Bill C-164 we find confirmation of the 1972 auditors, two separate firms of auditors for 1973 and one of those two firms for 1974.
As a new member, I cannot review past practices from experience, but I have had very detailed experience with auditors at another level of government and in private industry and I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this whole deal smells. It literally reeks to high heaven. Without questioning the capability of any of the auditors mentioned, I know that you do not change auditors without just cause, and having a former senior official with one audit company now a highly placed government employee, while I deplore and question the situation, is not just cause. Furthermore, under no circumstances do you appoint auditors, either new or in a continuing capacity, without the approval of the senior body, in this case the parliament of Canada. Appointing the auditors for 1972 retroactively in 1973 is highly questionable from a legal point of view, ridiculous from a practical point of view and smacks of arrogance in the extreme from the point of view of responsibility to the parliament and the people of Canada.
In 1973 we are asked to approve two sets of auditors. Obviously, one company is sufficient to complete the audit. Why, when, do we need two? The extra cost must be staggering. How much extra will probably be very difficult to ascertain. If the need for the third auditor is transitional, that is to say, while changing from one firm to another, surely we could have stayed with the second firm for a little longer since we have been adequately served by the first firm for many years.
If, on the other hand, the firm appointed for 1972 and jointly for 1973 has not been adequate, then the government should say so. If their services are adequate, even considering the involvement, directly or otherwise, of a past member of that firm in the Department of Transport, they should be kept on for a minimum of five years so that we can take advantage of their cumulative knowledge. These firms are of the highest calibre, and to be in the position of moving them around like pawns in a political chess game places them in an untenable position to the shame of the minister responsible. Or is the minister responsible? That is another question I shall expect to have answered.
For the moment, I do not intend to deal with the individual clauses of the bill; rather, I will go along with sending it to committee. But I assure the Minister of Transport that it will not be reported out of committee

At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that I have listened with a certain awareness to the comment of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Caouette) and I must note, concerning his proposals, that the dynastic aspect of politics are simply not transmitted through consanguinity, but through similar ideas. As we often say, like father, like son!

Before I begin my remarks, properly speaking, I might be allowed to make a couple of comments on what has gone on. I was intrigued by the intervention of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) proposing in some way that Air Canada be permitted to carry the can when it comes to air travel in Canada so that CP can pick up the chips. This reminds me of debates in the past with regard to the efficiency and profitability of the CN in relation to the CP. The poor old CN has always been the whipping-boy.
Canadian National is a public-owned railway. How useful it was for parties in this country, and I do not mean just political parties, to be able to refer to the CN as one horrible example of the effect of public ownership. Year after year we were told, "That is not the way to run a railroad; and besides, it loses money." Of course, it was never pointed out that the CNR does make money on the operational side but because it has to carry the debts of long ago its profit is quickly erased, so the poor old CNR winds up in the red.
My hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) gave the reasons this afternoon. Back in the twenties and early thirties, the government of the day picked up the can for a lot of its friends who had invested not too wisely in a number of railroads which were going into bankruptcy. It also picked up the tab to cover the losses of the private investors. To this day the CN is carrying the interest on these advances of a long time ago. It is no wonder the CN can rarely show a clear profit in its annual statements. Surely we could get around this business of partisan or political flummery by having the people of Canada, through this parliament, pick up this ancient debt and take it off the shoulders of the CN so that we can see once and for all whether a publicly-owned railway can operate efficiently.
However, even a cursory reading of the annual reports of the CN-and in case hon. members have not seen them, there is a resume at the back of the latest annual report- will show that as a publicly-owned corporation the CN is managing to show an operating profit. By comparison one can always point to the CP whose major function over the years has been to stick its fingers into the Canadian pie and pick up the plums. No wonder it is successful. With a deal of that kind, dating back to the early days of confederation, one would have to run an absolutely inefficient (Mr. Ellis.l
operation in order not to make money. The CP cannot help but make money. When I hear of the government offering yet more plums to the CP by way of airline routes to Milan, I can see the past repeating itself; I can see members of the opposition in years to come-and members of the government party, too, when it is their turn to be in opposition-berating the CN and Air Canada in relation to the profitability of the CPR and the CP Air operation.
Many years ago an American gentleman spoke forcefully about what was then called social democracy-socialism, as we know it today. He was asked whether he was in favour of government ownership of the railways. This is still a radical idea in the United States. This man, Eugene Debs, then said, "Gentlemen, I would rather have government ownership of the railroads than railroad ownership of the government." That is the nub of the question. I should like to speak for a few minutes about the investment policies of the CNR. Just because I believe in public enterprise does not mean I approve of everything this publicly-owned company, the CNR, does. As a matter of fact, there are many things it does of which
April 16, 1973

I disapprove. As a matter of fact, there are many things about this railway which I abhor. There are many aspects of the CNR which make it very hard to distinguish between it and a privately-owned enterprise. It behaves, in the main, like a privately-owned corporation no more evidently than in its investment policies.
A few weeks ago I had occasion to ask questions in the House about the CNR which was involved in investment in a project in Toronto established by Fidinam (Ontario) Limited. At that time the CNR pension fund had invested some $33 million in this particular development project. This $33 million was accompanied by a loan on the part of the Workmen's Compensation Board of Ontario in the amount of $15 million, all of which contributed to a total of $48 million supplied on the one hand by the public of Ontario-or, to put it more specifically, the working people of Ontario-and on the other hand by the public of Canada; or, to put ir more specifically, the working people of Canada, and even within that specificity, the people who work for the CNR.
Here we have an amount of $48 million for the purpose of building yet another high-rise office complex in the city of Toronto, as if we did not have too many already. One might say these moneys were advanced to a private corporation which in turn supplied a rather large amount of money of its own to build this project. But, surprise, surprise; this corporation which is totally foreign-owned- and for once it is not operating with American money but Italian money, although it is foreign money-received loans from the Canadian people, not from the stock exchanges, not from private dealers but from our publicly-owned corporation at the federal level, on the one hand, and a public institution at the provincial level, on the other hand, in the sum of $48 million to build this building the total worth of which is to be in the order of $53 to $55 million. That left a difference between $48 million and $53 million, so they turned around and went to Canadian private lenders to borrow this money.
We have here a situation of a foreign-owned corporation coming to this country, with nothing but gall and the stupidity and gullibility of parliament and the legislators of Canada, and setting up a development which it will control totally, having used almost none of its assets and mainly the assets of the Canadian public, and, more specifically, the assets put away for the old age of the Canadian workers across this country or the assets put away by workers in Ontario for protection against their disability at work.

My point received attention then, as I am sure it is now, because it is a massive, old-style political scandal. It was probably felt by members of the government party that I was insinuating that they, too, probably received some kind of benefit from the CNR pension fund loan to Fidinam. Nothing of the kind; I am sure they are clean. As a matter of fact, in answer to my question in the House the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Guay) said it was a perfectly legitimate transaction. Indeed it was. Under the law of Canada it was a perfectly legitimate thing for the CNR pension fund, which by the way is totally controlled by the investors of the CNR, to invest the workers' money in this enterprise without asking the workers.
What exactly was the scandal? It was not the fact that they may or may not have given something to the Liberal Party. I suspect they did not. As a matter of fact, if I were a member of the Liberal party I would be a bit annoyed if I did not get a cut of it. But that is not the point. The point is there are workers in Canada who need housing. As we all know, and as the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has said time and time again in this House, there is need for investment in housing.
Here we have a public fund that is dishing out money to a foreign corporation so it can set up yet one more totally useless high-rise office building right in the middle of Toronto where we do not need it. We have before us a bill which has to do with the capital allocation that this parliament is being asked to approve for the CNR. I think it is totally right and proper for us to ask just what the CNR intends to do with all this money. Sure, it would be very nice to say that it intends to offer better service to Canadians, that it intends to finally deliver the hopper cars to the west so that western farmers can move their wheat, or that it intends to bring back the old railway dining car.
You know, Mr. Speaker, I am getting on myself; I am well into my forties now. I look forward to the day when I can tell my grandchildren how it was in the good old days when we could travel on the railway and have a meal in the dining car. Those days are gone forever. Members of this House will be able to recount this story to their children, their grandchildren or their great grandchildren. But it is gone forever.
Sure, it would be nice to talk about the capitalization of the CNR for the provision of this kind of service. However, what I want to do tonight, and what other members of my party want to do in the days and nights to come, is to ask to what socially useful purpose for the benefit of the people of Canada will this money be used, because we have already had some horrible examples of the way the CNR uses its capital. A short while ago, had it not been for a mass reaction on the part of the people of Vancouver, the CNR, through its investment policies, would have lent money to a private corporation, the Four Seasons Hotel Corporation, to build a hotel on government property, which it would have bought from the government, right on the frontier boundary of Stanley Park in Vancouver. This is an example of total insensitivity to the needs of the people of Canada and to the value of a piece of property such as Stanley Park. So we must ask ourselves what the CNR intends to do with this money.

Recently the people of Canada, and particularly the people of Toronto, have been apprised of another wonderful project on the part of the CNR and its investment policies, namely, the Toronto CN tower. It is going to be a marvellous, wondrous project sticking up some 1,800 feet above lake level, whatever that is these days in Toronto, an it may not be very high as the lakes keep rising. It is to go up some 1,800 feet above lake level and it will be the first aspect of this vast development, backed by CNR, called metro centre right on the lakeshore of the city of Toronto.
I know that we the members from Toronto are accused of being parochial, that we are always talking about Toronto, but I would ask members of this House who come from other parts of the country to look very closely at the expenditure that CN investment policies intend to put into the city of Toronto. If I were from somewhere else I would be a little jealous, because that project now is slated to cost hundreds of millions of dollars. The CNR is in a kind of partnership with a private corporation, and Lord knows what the offspring of that coalition, if I may call it that, will be.
As the very first aspect of the project of metro centre, this obscene structure is to go up, namely, the CN communications tower. What is the true use of this tower? Oh, yes, we are told it is to be a wonderful new device to aid and abet electronic communications in the Toronto area. The CBC, I am told, will make use of its facilities. We could ask ourselves in this House why it was that as recently as two years ago the CBC spent so much money to refurbish and ameliorate its transmitter and antenna facilities in Toronto if it was simply going to move in as part of the CN tower a year or so afterwards.
The CN was supposed to go along with a partner in the building of the CN tower, but somehow or other the partner dropped out; perhaps because it was not a viable financial project. So we have the CN doing it alone. As you know, statements have been made by the pilots' associations of Canada to the effect that this tower will present a very real danger to air traffic over Toronto, particularly air traffic using Toronto island.
I do not have to tell you that if we intend to develop short take-off and landing air facilities in Canada, we will have to seriously consider using the Toronto island airport. I wonder how many members of this House from the Toronto area would like to take off in a STOL aircraft in what we call a misty day in Toronto, or come back late some Friday evening in mid-winter when the sky is somewhat unclear, knowing that the aircraft will somehow have to negotiate this tower which sticks up some 1,800 feet into the sky. The safety of this tower is really questionable, as is its presence in the Toronto air space.
The aspect of the tower with which I want to deal, however, is how interesting it is that the CN should decide that as the very first part of the metro centre development it should not build the new transportation centre, it should not build the new office complexes, it should not build the new residential housing which is supposed to go into that area-and I will have more to say on that later-but it should put up this tower. It is a cheap publicity trick.

Once the city of Toronto gives its approval, CN will begin building this tower in the spring. It was proposed that it be finished by 1974. That is a pretty hasty erection. The object of it is so that the people of Toronto will be told. "Look at the tower. Look at what we can do for you. Aren't you the proudest people in the world? You have this tower. We can build the rest of metro centre for you." This is a publicity gimmick, and nothing else. Millions of dollars will be spent to build this tower which will not be of any use to either the people of Toronto or the people of Canada.
How much will the tower cost? I do not know. As I read this bill, I see the amount on page 2. It reads; "CN Tower Limited, $8,800,000". I suspect that this bill is not up to date, because other figures have been quoted such as $18 million. I suspect that the figure of $8,800,000 includes only the part that was originally to be paid by CN when it was in partnership. I suspect that now we will have to carry the whole pack and it will be much more than $8,800,000 even at its inception, let alone at its completion.
I have said a few words about the metro centre and this is really what I would like to come to tonight. For members of the House who do not have the happy accident of being representatives of ridings in Toronto or the Toronto region, I think it is worth while pointing out that metro centre will cost several hundred million dollars. A development company has been set up to develop metro centre. For those of you whose familiarity with Toronto may be slight, let me point out that metro centre will be established south of what is now known as the Union station, which may be shortlived, and will extend to the lake. To the west it will be cheek-by-jowl with the park that was promised to us in Toronto as one of the election goodies of the present government.

Many questions have to be asked about this project. First: What consideration has been given by the developer, of which CN is a major partner, to the total urban development of the city of Toronto?
Any city has to bank upon its natural assets. The city of Montreal takes pride in having a mountain. In Toronto we have to look to the lake, and when I say "look to the lake"
I mean it because in most areas of Toronto you have to look very hard to be able to see the lake. We the residents and citizens of Toronto are separated from this great
April 16, 1973

natural asset by highways, railways, warehouses, factories, bakeries and commercial enterprises of many kinds.
Metro centre could be an extremely valuable and humane development if it were built so that families could live there, not just residents; because there are residents in Habitat, Montreal, right by the harbour but there are not many families. There are some real questions that have to be asked about the kinds of residential development which will be allowed in metro centre. There are other kinds of questions that have to be asked as to whether the city of Toronto really needs that much more office space. It is now a fact that in the city of Toronto the renting price of office space in older buildings is going down because we are beginning to have a surplus of new office areas. We have had a lot of building in the office realm and we should really ask ourselves whether it is really wise for the CNR to invest yet more money in this area.
There are questions to be asked about the location of the transportation centre itself in the metro centre development. At present we have a rather nice gare Union in Toronto. It is a place acclaimed by architects all over the continent as one of the finest examples of railway architecture in North America. It is a very fine building. There are very few buildings in this country, indeed on this continent, which have the sense of generosity of space that Toronto's Union station has. It is a superb railway terminal. The proposal contained in metro centre is to abandon the Union station as a railway station and to build a new transportation centre, as I understand it a little to the south and a little to the west of it.
The city of Toronto has built itself a subway which connects directly with the Union station, and it is an extremely useful arrangement that you can take the subway and go to the train terminal or to the Royal York hotel and take the bus to the airport. Mr. Speaker, let us ask ourselves how useful it will be for the people of Toronto to stop using the Union station as a transportation terminal and to have to go from the subway, from the main road arteries down to the new centre which will probably be extremely convenient for the CNR but not for the people of Toronto.
There are many questions of that kind to be asked about the capital project of the CNR involved in metro centre. But the last question I want to ask is perhaps the most important one. I ask: Where is the CNR going to get the money for the metro centre development? I have looked through the annual reports of the CNR and I have been trying to find some information about its investment policies. I find myself rather short of information. If I look at the list of officers, I can see that they have officers in charge of the investment division, including a chairman of the division and the general manager of the division. I looked through the annual reports, the latest of which I have is for 1971, and I find statements with regard to various aspects of the CNR financial operations. But I do not see very much about the CNR investment policies.
I challenge any member of this House to tell me whether he has been able to get out of the CNR any detailed information at all about the corporation's investment poli-
CNR and Air Canada
cies. As a matter of fact, you can probably get a little bit of information, if you are a good gleaner, from the statement on page 44 of the last report with regard to the pension trust fund. It gives a statement of its financial position as of December 31, 1971, and in very skimpy detail gives us the bare bones of CN's investment policies as far as its pension fund goes.
Globally, we have presented to us the figure of $255 million for mortgages. There is no more detail than that. If you tried to run a company in the private realm and presented a statement of this kind, you would be hauled before the securities commission of whichever province in which you were operating. This is not a statement. It is a fairy tale. And no wonder it has to be a fairy tale, because the CNR does not dare to detail to the people of Canada, to this parliament and to those workers whose money it directs to its own particular purposes the specific aspects of its investment policies. If it did, there might not be a resolution in Canada but there would be series of riots and rebellions in all centres of this country, rebellions which could not possibly be put down by any act of this parliament because they would be justified.
I want to end on this note, Mr. Speaker. Surely, if we have a public corporation which is responsible to this parliament we, as members of this House, should know in detail what its investment policies are and what are the purposes of these policies. And we should be able to decide the direction of the investment policies of this corporation. First of all, it is a public corporation. Secondly, it is a large corporation; and when I say large, I want members of the House to realize that just one aspect of this corporation, the CNR pension fund, has control over some $1.36 billion at this time-and that ain't hay!
Mr. Speaker, I hope to hear later from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), whose bill in a sense this is, and from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand)-I would even be willing to hear from the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport-on the investment policies of the CNR and what it is doing in particular with the money it has gleaned over the years from the men who have dedicated their lives to the operation of this publicly-owned corporation in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad I received a little clap when I rose to speak, because I do not think this is going to be a very exciting speech. I want to say something tonight about my home city, Calgary, in reference to the depot there. That city, in my opinion and in the opinion of the 450,000 people living in it, serves the southern part of Alberta, the resource industry, the ranching industry, the farming industry; and we have been neglected.
On January 23 last we saw some light. An announcement was made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) in which he said a new $57.7 million air terminal complex would be built in Calgary over the next three years. No one can quarrel with that. But I ask, when will it be finished? The need is great. The initial work is scheduled to begin in the summer of 1973 and it will not be complete until 1976. I plead with the minister to start the project now. There is unemployment in Canada, but above all there is serious need, in the heart of what we call the oil capital of western Canada, for a new air depot because
3352

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
of the inadequacy of the present one to serve the travelling public and the people who work in Air Canada, CPA and the Department of Transport.
Here is the history of the present depot. At the beginning of the 1950s the air depot was owned by the municipal body. The airport, like other airports, was owned by the Department of Transport. It was a nice depot; in fact, it was the talk of Canada at that time. Because it suited the existing need, nothing further was done. Since that time, all across the country-at Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, London, Windsor, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Vancouver, Regina and Saskatoon-the DOT has built new depots to serve the travelling public who use Air Canada and CPA. Then in 1965-it might have been in 1964-an agreement was made between the city of Calgary and DOT by which the latter purchased the depot from the municipality.
At that time the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill was minister of transport, and he promised that Calgary would immediately get a new air depot because of the inadequate size of the existing depot. The deal was consummated, the money was paid to the city, and the city looked to the federal government of the day-and is still looking to the federal government-for action. This air depot is something like the Saskatchewan dam. For years Jimmy Gardiner promised a dam for Saskatchewan, but it was not built until John Diefenbaker became prime minister. We have been waiting and waiting for action on the air depot.
In 1969, things became desperate. When I read the figures, hon. members will understand why. I am going to make a good case and, I hope, influence the minister. I put the following question on the order paper, which was answered by the minister on February 19, 1973. Question No. 428 reads as follows;
1.	When will the construction of Calgary's new federal air depot at the international airport commence, and when will it be completed?
2.	How many people used the Calgary international airport depot for the year 1972, for the purpose of leaving or coming (a) into Calgary (b) into Edmonton (c) into Winnipeg?
3.	In 1972, what was the number of commercial airplanes that landed and took off from the (a) Calgary international airport (b) Edmonton international airport (c) Winnipeg international airport?
The answers can be found at page 1393 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker. Edmonton has such a large airport, and it is built so far out of town, that you could almost say it was in Red Deer. The only figures available are for 1971. These were given to me by the Minister of Transport, and I know they are accurate because I checked them. At Calgary international airport 985,375 people either took off or landed. Edmonton airport has a corridor where you walk so far that you can never see the end of it. It is deep in the country. There were 100,000 less people leaving than arriving, and 866,340 people used the airport for both arrivals and departures. Winnipeg, which is called the gateway to the west, was used by only 856,000 people.
These figures show that Calgary is a very busy international airport. In 1969, the situation was so desperate that you could hardly move in or out of the airport, and since then several millions of dollars have been spent to erect temporary buildings. Everybody here knows what. that

means; the Department of National Defence is still using the temporary buildings erected in the Second World War.
Mr. Speaker, I invite every member of the House to come to Calgary for Easter-come to Lake Louise or Banff and enjoy the beauty and the atmosphere. But what is happening today? Under the new rules of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), 44 RCMP will be stationed in the depot at all times. The congestion is such that when you walk up some sort of ramp to the second floor, only six chairs are available for 112 people. The government must have thought they were building cattle pens. The area is heated by an electric heater which is likely to burn you.
The security check is impossible. Passengers are crowded in like cattle and are told that anyone without a handbag or briefcase can go through; they separate people into carriers and non-carriers. Passengers are then herded into this pen, and as a Member of Parliament you pray that you get on first-class. You wait days to get a reservation out of Calgary and I am told you wait four or five days to get out of Regina. For two summers there was no air-conditioning. Employees did not want to petition because some were employed by DOT, some by Air Canada and some by CPA and all are dependent on the government to get things organized. I must give credit to the former minister of transport, because when I complained last summer they did get some form of air-conditioning.
There are no facilities for the aged, the infirm or the sick. There are no wheelchairs and anybody who cannot walk must board the plane on a stretcher. I see that the minister is rubbing his eyes. I wish he had been here when I congratulated him for at least making the statement to which I referred. I am very serious, Mr. Speaker. I know the minister is a hard worker and a dedicated man, but I hope he will make a personal visit at Easter if possible. I will see to it that he gets the best hospitality from the Chamber of Commerce and from the mayor. I am told that the mayor is a Liberal. I hope the minister can promise to get matters moving during 1973, and completed before 1976. The present conditions are not the fault of this minister; he inherited the problems. But the one million people using the airport are trying to get service.
The working conditions there are a disgrace, not only to the city of Calgary but to the province and to Canada. It is worse than the airport we used to have at Ottawa. When President Eisenhower landed here and looked around, he thought he was in the wilderness. Calgary is the centre of the resource industries, people come there from the United States, France, Germany, Britain and all over the world to deal in petroleum and natural gas. The airport is busier than Edmonton or Winnipeg, and is as busy if not busier than Vancouver, yet it has the poorest facilities. It is totally inadequate for the people being served by the airlines, and it is totally inadequate for the employees. No other city would put up with it. It is totally unacceptable to the workers, to Air Canada and to CPA and should be totally unacceptable to the DOT workers in Calgary or to any other corporate body.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot wait until 1976. In the minister's news release of January 23, 1973, he said:
Initial preparatory work is scheduled to begin in the summer of 1973.
April 16, 1973

I am always frightened by that word "begin".
When it is completed early in 1976-
If I know anything about government projects-it does not matter whether they are NDP, Conservative or Liberal, provincial or federal; they are all the same-it is generally two years later.
-the terminal will be capable of handling up to two million passengers a year.
I believe that will be 1976 or 1978. We have one million passengers now, and by then there will be two million. They will have to truck them to the planes because they cannot use this depot. I cannot speak with any more feeling than I have tonight. We are spending $2 billion on unemployment insurance; everybody is crying about it and making politics out of it. We should take that money and get this project moving. In 1939, when this country was at war, things were built overnight. If this can be done in times of crisis, why can't it be done in peacetime? Why do we have to drag our feet?
Calgary needs an airport. We have the money and the know-how, and people are looking for jobs. Why does the minister not show that he is a man of aggression and that he loves western Canada? If the airport is built, even Pat Mahoney will not lose his deposit the next time.

I must relate what happened to someone I consider to be a fair minded man. He became so frustrated that he left a suit of clothing in the depot. The following day he contacted Air Canada and they located the suit. The only way he could get the suit from Air Canada was to pay an express charge of $8. Do you know who that gentleman is? Me. I
CNR and Air Canada
was not very hospitable toward those dedicated public servants.
The people at the Toronto airport have a great sense of humour. During the course of the argument a fellow came up to me and said that if I had any trouble I should take it up with my Member of Parliament. I finally realized what little power and what little force we have. Maybe the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was right when he referred to strawmen and said they were nobodies. What about the people who have not been elected to parliament? What kind of service do they get?
