speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for me this is the fifth annual event on the CN financing bill. I know the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has taken part in this debate for many more years than that. I have been party to this kind of debate four years out of five, because in one year the bill was not passed. What strikes me as strange is that we always lose sight of the main thrust and purpose of the bill. I have been as guilty as any other member in complaining about the schedules, the terminals of Air Canada and the train service. This is a good opportunity to do that. However, the real point is not mentioned. Each year we go through this exercise and vote funds, not only for the capitalizing of the Canadian National Railways' system and Air Canada but to cover deficits of the CN system.
Under successive old-style governments it has been a tradition since 1923 to establish a public corporation to which they pay lip service and then refuse to let it function as it can and should. They handicap it with a debt structure that makes it impossible for it to succeed in any meaningful way in terms of providing service to the public. The hon. member for Calgary North wonders and worries about the inadequacies of terminal capacity, baggage handling, and so forth, in his city. I defy him to name any private corporation that could or would operate under the financial handicaps the CN system has had since 1923.
We are saddled with a corporation, regardless of whether it is privately or publicly-owned, which started off with the deck stacked against it. In its beginning it was saddled with the debts of bankrupt railways which private enterprise could not operate. We are still paying those debts. In the course of being saddled with the debts of five or six bankrupt railroads which were brought into the CN system, including the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific. On top of having their annual capitalization, they have always been saddled with the original debt of these bankrupt companies.
I do not pretend to be an expert in this area, but it seems that the remaining $1,900 million public debt on the CNR books should be taken over by the government of Canada in return for shares that may or may not pay 3 per cent or

April 16, 1973
CNR and Air Canada
4 per cent per year. They should remove forever the handicap that our publicly-owned rail and air transportation system have had, particularly CNR.
We go through this exercise every year. In previous years I have heard the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) talk about the glories of the CPR because it makes a profit. He and some members of the official opposition seem to forget that most years CN has had an operating profit. I believe the last figures shows a net operating profit of approximately $50 million. However, the interest on the debt which goes back to 1923 was $72 million. Parliament had to vote an additional $22 million or $23 million because the interest on that debt ate up the net operating funds plus an appropriation from parliament.
In 1923, the railroads of the day, all of which were privately owned, were in financial difficulties; they were going belly up. That is the problem we were faced with. But why pass this burden on to a succeeding railroad which is owned and operated on behalf of the people of Canada? If we feel that as a nation we have some kind of financial obligation to pay off the bonds of bankrupt railroads-and I do not agree we have-why impose this liability on a succeeding railroad which is publicly-owned?
Believe it or not, there are still $4 million worth of bonds on the books of the CN which can never be paid off unless a special act of parliament is passed, because they are held in perpetuity-3 per cent interest in perpetuity. That is a long time. It is even longer than never. But these bonds of indebtedness are still a burden on the back of the CNR.
No corporation, public or private, can operate outside the limits of government policy. It can only operate as well as government policy will allow. And while we all have complaints about rail services, branch line abandonment, station agencies, air terminals or air traffic schedules, these are only a small part of the total picture. Unless and until parliament is prepared to make fundamental changes in the direction and purpose of national transportation policy, we shall continue to go through this exercise each year, and each year we shall vote $20 million or $30 million more to pick up the deficit of the CN system to pay off the indebtedness with which the railway was saddled, almost $2 billion, in 1923.
Another aspect of the tragedy brought to mind by the annual exercise we go through in considering the CN financing bill is this. The CN, which is publicly-owned, is a convenient victim of all the brickbats and complaints of Members of Parliament and the public. The CP has yet to answer for some of its actions perpetrated at the expense of the public. We cannot get at the CPR. I would hope that in this parliament, with the help of an excellent and respected chairman of the transport committee, officials of the Canadian Pacific will appear before the Standing Committee on Transportation and Communications, for the first time in about seven years, because we have some questions to ask these gentlemen. It is entirely unfair. I must confess to some feelings of guilt about this myself. We tend to take too much out at the expense of the CN because of the occasion provided by the annual CN financ-

ing bill. Too often it is the CP which has led the way in abandoning branch lines or making applications to close stations.
I think we have been very fortunate in the kind of employees and managerial people we have in both the CN and Air Canada. We are fortunate they have not quit on us. What we are doing to Air Canada right now, in terms of national air policy vis-a-vis Canadian Pacific Airlines, is equivalent to what we have been doing all along to the CN vis-a-vis the CPR.
Air Canada is supposed to have exclusive access to Europe, the Caribbean and the Atlantic routes and supposedly CP Air, under the Orwellian-Pickersgillian policy, was to have exclusive rights in the Pacific and South America. But over the period of years since the fifties the picture has been altered. CP Air has been given rights to Lisbon and Madrid. By golly, the next thing we knew it obtained rights to Amsterdam. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is likely to recommend to the cabinet that it be given the route to Milan, Italy, In fact, I would be prepared to bet the minister a crock that this is what he will do. I would be happy to lose that bet.
Air Canada should be getting the new routes to Italy, the new landing sites in Germany, and extended routes the government could negotiate to Greece, the Middle East and to Asia. I doubt they will get them. I suspect they could get exchange routes with the Russians to Moscow and maybe to Siberia. But this landing site in Italy will go to CP, I will bet a nickel. I will take that bet up with the minister as well. But when Air Canada asks for a share of rights in the Pacific, the answer is; "Oh, no; those are reserved for CP Air," after all, that has been national air policy for the past 15 years. Surely, if it is logical to let CP Air erode the viability and the profitability of Air Canada in the Atlantic and on European routes, Air Canada is entitled to routes to the Pacific rim countries. We cannot get a word out of the minister or the government on that score.
It seems to me it would be logical to let Air Canada take routes to the Philippines and to India in both directions or, if you like, in one direction all the way around the world. The government and its predecessors of both stripes, right and far right, have continually handicapped our public corporations by imposing policies which make it impossible for them to succeed. We have continued to syphon off some of the best routes Air Canada had, giving them to CP Air or to regional carriers which have government heelers on their boards of directors. Air Canada suffers as a result, and the public complains about its usefulness.
I wish this government, or some government, would leave a clear field for a publicly-owned corporation answerable to parliament to operate under conditions of really open competition with private carriers answerable only to their boards of directors. I should like to see that kind of fight. I was hoping that the Minister of Transport would have been willing to engage in that kind of fight. Our national transport policy since 1967 mitigates against the publicly-owned corporation and on every occasion the CN or Air Canada have been succeeding, or on the verge of succeeding, there seems to have been a move to say, "Well fellows; that is far enough. Let somebody else have this, the CP, or Trans Air, or Quebec Air or Nordair." They
April 16, 1973

would not operate when they could have had the routes by themselves, but they came in afterwards to get the gravy.
This is what the bill before us is all about. We can raise questions in committee about terminals or schedules or branch line abandonment, but unless there is a national transportation policy which allows publicly owned carriers to function as they could and should function, the things we are complaining about are only the results of the failure to approach the subject in a basically satisfactory way. Since confederation, the Canadian economy as a whole, and more particularly Canadians isolated or nearly so by their geographical situation, have had to pay too high a price both individually or as part of an enterprise for transportation either of themselves or of their goods to other areas in Canada.
Where transportation is privately-owned, it must operate on the basis of making a profit. If it is publicly-owned, it has to operate on the basis of profitability first, and the provision of services has to come second. Privately-owned enterprises have to make a profit. That is the only reason for their existence. If transportation enterprises are publicly-owned and are required to operate on the basis of profitability, they cannot provide adequate service in a country with our kind of climate and geography. It is an illusion to think we can maintain a national air and rail transport system when the motive for operation is profitability. I submit this has resulted in an inefficient service to the public and a discriminatory transportation system which fails to meet the needs of the Canadian economy as well as the convenience of individuals. Our publicly-owned air system has been prevented from doing a better job by depriving them of lucrative routes. The government has already helped private carriers by handing them new routes, particularly international routes, which really means CPA.
I have been here for only five years. Many members in this place have been here for 20 or 25 years. It has been our repeated plea that we need a national transportation policy which is made in Canada, one which takes into account our geography and climate. Our 1967 National Transportation Act needs to be drastically revised to the point where the provision of transportation services-I emphasize the word "services"-rail, air, pipelines, etc., takes priority over whether or not those services are economic or profitable. A national transportation policy that takes into account the geography of the country, as I have said, a transportation policy that equalizes costs to as great a degree as possible for the delivery of goods and people, is what is required.
We must also include in this policy, communications, equalized and/or subsidized freight, express, telecommunications and passenger fares. Other countries have been doing this-northern countries-for decades. We are still trying to operate a transportation system on policies out of the 1890s taken from our neighbour to the south. Even there the great private enterprise system of the United States has been going belly up over the last ten years. They now have a system that is publicly-controlled and operated so far as passenger services are concerned in a complex of seven or so large U.S. railroads, but even this is
CNR and Air Canada
not succeeding because they have gone about it by adopting half measures.
We must treat transportation as an essential public utility and think of it in that way, because public utilities operate best for the public, in that it takes priority over the demands or considerations of boards of directors, shareholders, or for that matter members of Parliament. If we are not prepared to have a National Transportation Act that has this central theme and thrust, we will continue on down the road we have been travelling and lose three or four thousand miles of rail lines on the prairies. We will lose upward of five to six hundred agencies all across Canada. We will lose a viable air transportation system that is publicly-owned because it will continue to be eroded. We will see our publicly-owned transportation systems paying attention to shopping centres and high-rise office buildings while trains are later and airports cannot handle our baggage. All of this calls for the public ownership of rail and air transportation facilities and pipelines. Many other countries that have been very strongly free enterprise-oriented did this years ago and have transportation systems from which we can learn something.
My second point, which I should like to hear about from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) before the debate on second reading concludes, concerns the government giving some kind of undertaking or commitment that some $1,900 million of the old debt of the CNR will be taken over by the government of Canada in return for an equivalent value of shares in the Canadian National system, so that the system is entirely owned by the public of Canada through this parliament. Thereafter, there will be no more interest on debts amounting to $20 million to $30 million a year in excess of the operating profits of our own rail transportation system.
Further, I submit that our air transportation systems, both national and international, have to be publicly-owned and operated. Further, we want a commitment or undertaking from the Minister of Finance before this bill receives second reading that there will be a further moratorium on rail line abandonment, as well as a moratorium on the closure of agencies and the establishment of the so-called customer service centres. There must be a massive expenditure to improve transportation facilities and to substantially expand their capability, as well as use made of ports like Churchill and Prince Rupert. We will expect to hear something about all these matters from the Minister of Finance before concluding the second reading stage of this debate.

subtopic: POLLUTION-QU'APPELLE LAKES, SASK.- IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS IN REPORT
POLLUTION-QU'APPELLE LAKES, SASK.- IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS IN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 30 I directed two questions to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) concerning the implementation of the Qu'Appelle board study report, a study carried out by the department in co-operation with the governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. At that time Mr. Speaker indicated that if there was urgency, the subject could be debated at the time of adjournment.
The Qu'Appelle basin study was started in 1970, the report was completed in 1972 and it was made public in January, 1973. The report makes two main types of recommendations, long-term recommendations and those which require swift implementation. That report makes clear that sewage from the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw, and the Canadian forces base is the principal cause of the decay of the lakes in the Qu'Appelle River system.
It is estimated that about 2.8 million pounds of nitrogen and 2.2 million pounds of phosphates are being dumped into the system annually, 70 per cent of it from these sources. This is a situation that must be remedied if the Qu'Appelle lakes are to be saved. What is required is that these two cities upgrade their sewage treatment facilities in order to remove these nutrients from the effluent before it is discharged into the river system.
The report estimates the total cost of effluent control for which immediate action is recommended at $15 million, half of which would be required to instal the necessary treatment facilities at Regina and Moose Jaw. Clearly, a financial commitment of this scope will be difficult, if not impossible, to manage at the municipal level.
The Qu'Appelle valley and its lakes and rivers represent an irreplaceable national asset as important to the people of Saskatchewan as the Fraser River system is to the people of British Columbia. However, the financial burden of solving the pollution problem of the Qu'Appelle is for the most part being left by the federal government to these two cities.
The minister can boast, as he did in Vancouver on February 5, that his department has spent almost $40 million on sewage treatment works in British Columbia since 1970, but when asked what he intends to do in Saskatchewan he remains strangely silent. Is it any wonder that the federal Liberal party has become a rejected and discredited political party in the prairie provinces of western Canada, given this kind of attitude by its ministers?
The situation calls for leadership from the Department of the Environment and a sense of urgency in the implementation of this report. What is being demonstrated is not a sense of urgency but a sense of inertia and drift. The citizens of Regina will pay their share of the cost of these facilities and more, but to expect them to provide sewage treatment facilities at a higher level than any other major centre in Canada, which is the case, without substantial assistance from senior government is just not reasonable.

The Hon. Jack Davis is prepared to recommend that we make available to Saskatchewan the same assistance that we have provided to the province of Ontario through the Great Lakes agreement, that is, to ensure that sufficient funds are available through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation fund so that the loans to the municipalities, which have a 25 per cent forgiveness feature, will be readily available.
In addition, as with the Great Lakes agreement we are prepared to share on a 50-50 basis with the province of Saskatchewan any costs which might be involved in pilot plant construction and operation that may be required to determine the most efficient type of treatment to deal with the nutrient problem at Regina and Moose Jaw.

subtopic: INCOME TAX-PRACTICE OF DISCOUNTING TAX REBATE CHEQUES-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT REGULATION
INCOME TAX-PRACTICE OF DISCOUNTING TAX REBATE CHEQUES-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT REGULATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over a year ago I first drew the attention of this House to a practice which members in all parts of the House found deplorable. I refer to the practice of discounting government cheques. I think it would be worth while to take a moment to explain this term. It is possible in most major centres in this country, and it would seem especially so in western Canada where such enterprises advertise in daily newspapers, if someone is in desperate need of money and is guaranteed receipt in the future of a government cheque such as for unemployment insurance, old age pension or as an income tax rebate, to secure what amounts to a loan with the anticipated cheque as security. However, the procedure followed is for the lender in effect to purchase the cheque at a reduced amount. That is the reason for the term "discounting".
Thus, if someone anticipates receiving an income tax rebate, say in the amount of $500, and there is solid evidence to support his expectation, a discounting operation might offer such a person $350 in cash, half now and half on receipt of the cheque, in return for the total cheque being turned over to the business offering the cash. The amount discounted, if computed as interest on an annual basis, would customarily amount to 1,000 per cent to 2,000 per cent.
The operator of such a discounting operation encounters little or no risk because before providing the cash he requires definite guarantees that the government will, in fact, be issuing the cheque in question. Moreover, he usually requires that arrangement be made for the cheque in question to be sent to his address rather than to the address of the person to whom it is nominally payable. Interest at the rate of 1,000 per cent to 2,000 per cent for a loan involving no risk to the lender can only be termed usury.
I raised this question last year in connection with the discounting of unemployment insurance cheques. I am sure that other members, while they may not have done so in the House, have made private representations to the minister. As a result of these efforts, the Unemployment Insurance Commission established new regulations which had the effect of preventing the use of an address not that of a claimant under the unemployment insurance plan without the permission of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This did much to correct the situation with respect to Unemployment Insurance Commission cheques.
Further, I am given to understand the government instituted legal proceedings against one such loansharking operation in Alberta as a test case. One of the series of question which I asked on March 7 which has given rise to the debate this evening was of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) asking him the status of that case. He took the question as notice and undertook to report to me privately. I am still waiting for the information and would hope that whoever replies this evening will present it to the House.
Beyond that I asked, in order to end such deplorable practices as they affect income tax rebates, if the Department of National Revenue was contemplating action similar to that taken by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. My question received a very sympathetic but
Adjournment Debate
unenlightening response from the minister. If I had time I would quote his answer because it provokes three further questions which I hope might be answered this evening. First, does the prevention of such practice require an amendment to the Income Tax Act and, if so, does the government intend to introduce such an amendment, and when?
Second, can charges be laid against such usurers? However, such a question is not permissible since one cannot demand a legal opinion of a minister, so I would simply ask whether the government intends pressing charges against such operators? Third, has the Department of National Revenue taken steps to prevent the mailing of an income tax rebate cheque to an address other than that of the intended recipient without departmental approval, in line with the action of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, as opposed to preventing the making of cheques payable to anyone but the taxpayer?
I ask these questions because each of them involves action which the government could immediately undertake to curtail these usurious practices. Their elimination, I believe, could be accomplished by amending the Small Loans Act in the manner I have suggested in a bill now before the House. Bill C-57, standing in my name, would change the definition of a loan in the definition section of the bill to include the practice of discounting an amount of $1,500 or under. Thus, the interest on loans against the future receipt of the government cheque under the amount of $1,500 would be limited to 2 per cent a month, or 24 per cent a year, as opposed to the 1,000 per cent to 2,000 per cent per annum now customarily charged in such transactions.
Thus, my final question is: Is such legislation being contemplated by the government? The BNA Act, section 91, subsection 18, "Bills of exchange and promissory notes" and subsection 19, "Interest", clearly gives the federal government authority so to act, and I hope they will.
To recapitulate, my questions are as follows. First, what is the current status of the legal proceedings against discounters instituted by the government of Canada? Second, is an amendment to the Income Tax Act required to prevent such practices with respect to income tax rebates and, if so, when may we expect to receive such legislation? Third, if the Income Tax Act already permits charges to be laid against such loan sharks, when may we expect such action to be taken? Fourth, has the Department of National Revenue taken steps to prevent the mailing of a rebate cheque to an address other than that of the taxpayer concerned? Fifth, is the government considering an amendment to the Small Loans Act having the effect of bringing the practice of discounting on amounts under $1,500 under its provisions and, if so, when may we expect such legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Stanbury (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: INCOME TAX-PRACTICE OF DISCOUNTING TAX REBATE CHEQUES-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT REGULATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) for raising this question and giving me the opportunity to indicate the concern, which the government shares, about the practices of discounting government cheques. I wish that the answers and the solutions to

April 16, 1973
Adjournment Debate
the problem were as simple as those suggested by the hon. member.
There are, of course, a number of alternatives, one of which he suggested and which I have asked my officials and those in other departments to consider, because I do agree with him that it is a deplorable practice in many cases. But there is, of course, a possibility that people will innocently and in all good faith wish to enter into transactions with regard to government cheques as they do with other financial paper, and there is a question as to how restrictive we should be in preventing this practice. There are obviously some Canadians who wish to deal with government cheques in this way. Personally, I think they are unwise to do so.
In the case of income tax refunds, we are now aiming for the fastest possible processing of them, and in cases where income tax returns are properly completed there should be a refund in the hands of the taxpayer within approximately six weeks of the filing of the return where a refund is called for. Therefore, I might say to any taxpayer who has attempted to discount his refund that there is no reason to do so, the refund will be in his hands almost as quickly as if he were to deal with the discounter.
I have asked my officials to watch closely the returns which appear to be filed by discounters. It is questionable whether we should prevent refunds being sent to addresses other than those of the taxpayer, because there are many financial institutions in Canada in whose hands taxpayers have placed their financial affairs. There is some question about whether or not we should prevent their doing that.
Of course, one possibility is that provincial governments, including that of the province from which the hon. member comes, could deal with this matter on the basis of licensing and provincial law which, I might say, is somewhat clearer than the jurisdiction of the federal government in this respect. There was a prosecution by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, as the hon. member mentioned, which I believe was unsuccessful at the first stage and is under appeal. This illustrates the difficulty, under federal legislation, of proceeding against these practices.
I would urge the hon. member to exercise his influence on the provincial government of his own province to take action within its jurisdiction to curb such practices. In the meantime, my officials are exploring all possible avenues, including the one suggested by the hon. member, and if it appears that the federal government can properly restrain this kind of practice, I hope to propose a method of doing so or have one of my colleagues do so in the House at a later date.
It is matter of some complexity. We want to be sure that we do not unfairly restrict or restrain the ability of Canadians to deal with their own property, and particularly we want to avoid infringing upon the powers of the provinces in this respect. But I share the hon. member's concern. We will keep it under very close observation and we hope to achieve the same objective that he has in mind.

subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURE-MULTICULTURALISM-POLICY OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
CANADIAN CULTURE-MULTICULTURALISM-POLICY OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak on the matter of the sale of radio station CKSB, St. Boniface, to the publicly-owned Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is not that I want to question or criticize the sale, but rather I want to take this opportunity to present to the Secretary of State responsible for multicul-turalism, some of the viewpoints that multicultural groups have in respect to the use of the CBC and the broadcasting of multicultural programs.
CKSB was a privately-owned French station in Manitoba. In fact, it was owned by the parish of St. Boniface. In the last number of years, because of financial difficulties and other reasons the board of directors of CKSB sold air time to various multicultural groups for the broadcasting of programs which were specifically directed to multicultural groups in the Winnipeg and southern Manitoba area. Communities such as Polish, Ukrainian, German, Jewish, Portuguese and Italian used the radio station for these purposes, and the co-operation between the radio station and these various groups was exemplary.
There is a need for a second language radio station in Manitoba, a need which radio station CKSB was fulfilling. But because of the financial difficulties which the station was experiencing, the CBC stepped in and made a purchase offer to the board of directors and on March 29, 1973, the Canadian Radio-Television Commission approved the sale of the radio station. CKSB, now being a CBC-owned radio station, is to fulfill the following requirements:
The commission will therefore expect the station, as will be specified in the conditions of the licence, to complement network service with a substantial amount of programming originating from and designed for the French-speaking residents of this area.
I endorse this policy because the people in my riding have among them proportionately the second highest number of French-speaking Manitobans, and radio station CKSB, broadcasting in the French language, serves a vital purpose for these people. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, because of the policy of the CBC that it can only be used in the French or English language as far as broadcasting is concerned, these various multicultural groups which availed themselves of the services of CKSB now find themselves having to look elsewhere for broadcast privileges.
On February 22, 1973, as noted at page 1547 of Hansard,! asked the Minister of State in charge of multiculturalism (Mr. Haidasz) the following question, in part, with regard to the sale of CKSB:
As there are no hearings scheduled for Winnipeg on this matter, can the minister indicate to the House what alternatives he is proposing which would preserve the established customary rights of multicultural groups in the Winnipeg area?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of government policy and if anything is to be done it will be announced in the usual way.
I am still waiting for that policy, Mr. Speaker. In a sense, the CRTC made policy on an interim basis, because on the announcement of the sale of CKSB to the CBC the commission stated:

The CBC has informed the commission that, in view of this long standing practice, broadcast time will continue to be made available on a similar basis to any of these groups desiring it for a period of 12 months in order to provide sufficient time for those groups which have not already done so to make other suitable arrangements for their programming in the Winnipeg area. The commission considers this to be a reasonable and equitable proposal.
I commend the commission for giving the government 12 months to set its house in order. But I am still waiting for the government to clearly state its policy on CBC in relation to its position on multicultural programming.
I have a recommendation to make which I hope the parliamentary secretary will convey to the Secretary of State. It is that the CBC should establish a policy whereby these various multicultural groups could use a certain number of broadcast hours for the purpose of multicultural broadcasting. I know that the Secretary of State has been approached by various multicultural groups with this request.
There are radio stations in southern Manitoba such as CFAM-CHSM, which has been exemplary in giving time to multicultural groups to broadcast in the language of the background of the people. We are asking that the people who came here and who are not Francophone or Anglophone, but who became Canadians and good citizens, have the right to some time on CBC in order to maintain their cultural heritage. This is not divisive but is simply a matter of maintaining a heritage. I suggest that in western Canada, at least, these are the groups that have given us a cultural mosaic and a special identity which should be preserved. I suggest that the government should seriously consider a policy whereby the CBC, within a relatively short time, should make time available for multicultural broadcasting.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURE-MULTICULTURALISM-POLICY OF CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to my hon. friend's
Adjournment Debate
question, I could easily refer him to the reply given by the Secretary of State, but I think to reply thus would be inadequate, and in view of the importance of this matter, I ought to add a few comments.
Although Section 38 of the Official Languages Act deals with the rights and privileges of other languages, I would point out to the hon. member that, in the case he is particularly concerned with, the multilingual broadcasting privileges that this population enjoys were not given to them by the government organization but by a private station. The broadcasting act is explicit on this point, and CBC policy follows it closely. The member is also aware that a lot remains to be done in the field of broadcasting in the two official languages of Canada: there are places where there is no service in French or English, or where these must be improved, which are assignments of major importance for the CBC, and will continue to take priority until all such projects have been realized.
The CBC Board of Directors is acutely aware of the growing need to fulfill the special needs of the different regions, and there is a close link between regional and ethnic programming. The CBC considers that at the present time, its national broadcasting service is not suitable for multilingualism and that the best solution to the problem of programs of an ethnic nature would be for the ethnic groups to continue to try to obtain broadcasting time on a local basis, from stations that do not belong to the network, so that the CBC can concentrate on its major obligations.
The hon. member stressed the CRTC's decision to extend these rights for a year, and I do not intend to comment on this. I can assure my hon. friend that I am convinced, from the way that he dealt with the problem, that he has made some very serious suggestions, and that I shall hasten to inform the minister tomorrow of all his remarks, and we will try to find an equitable solution to the really serious problems which he has brought up.
